Facts:
[1] There is no agreement among practitioners and in the literature on the precise definition of mixed reality (MR).
[2] The dictionary definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a medium consisting of immersive computer-generated environments in which elements of physical and virtual environments are combined, but this definition is not categorical about how MR differs from virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR).
[3] One definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR comprises everything in between the two extremes of the reality-virtuality continuum, the real environment and the virtual environment, so augmented reality (AR) is included in this broader definition of MR.
[4] Another definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR denotes the capability to combine augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) technologies in the same application or on the same device, so such a combined application is called MR from a developer's point of view.
[5] Another definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a strong version of augmented reality (AR), meaning a more capable version of augmented reality that has an advanced understanding of the physical environment and may be bound to specific hardware.
[6] In one definition used by many people, mixed reality (MR) is a synonym for augmented reality (AR), because in both cases the user views reality augmented or enhanced with digital content overlaid on the view of reality, and can interact with that content.
[7] Because most definitions of mixed reality (MR) are confusing and the controversy is not needed for this course, the course assumes that MR is the same technology as augmented reality (AR) and treats the two terms as interchangeable.

[1] The basic research phase of augmented reality (AR) came after the experimentation phase and included much influential work in the 1990s that shaped the field of augmented reality.
[2] Tom Caudell is often credited with coining the phrase augmented reality (AR) because he published the first academic article containing the term AR in 1992.
[3] During the basic research phase of augmented reality (AR), research projects at the University of North Carolina included registration tracking techniques in 1993 and 1994, early research in 1995 and 1996 on see-through head-mounted displays typically used in AR, and several applications developed alongside the basic research.
[4] During the basic research phase of augmented reality (AR), research at Columbia University included one of the first academic papers on AR describing the KARMA system in 1993, work in 1993 on AR interaction methods, that is, how to interact with augmented digital content, and some publications on mobile AR systems in 1997.
[5] During the basic research phase of augmented reality (AR), research at the University of Toronto included overlaying virtual cues on stereoscopic video from 1991 to 1993 and work on AR applications from 1992 to 1993.
[6] Chameleon was an early handheld or mobile augmented reality (AR) system developed in 1993 that allowed a user to move a liquid-crystal display (LCD) over a piece of paper and see virtual content.
[7] NaviCam by Rekimoto was a handheld or mobile augmented reality (AR) system developed in 1995 that superimposed virtual tags on real objects using handheld and head-mounted displays.
[8] Chameleon and NaviCam were true augmented reality (AR)-type applications and precursors to the kind of AR applications seen today.

Course XR, segment goal: Define immersion and explain six qualities: extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, plot-informing.
Facts:
[1] In definition originally proposed by Slater and Wilbur, immersion is the objective degree to which a virtual reality (VR) system and application projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in a way that is extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing.
[2] Extensive, as a quality of immersion, refers to the range of sensory modalities presented to the user, with examples including visual, auditory, physical force perception, smell, taste, and touch, and the more sensory organs are stimulated by computer-provided stimuli, the more extensive the immersion is.
[3] Matching, as a quality of immersion, refers to congruence between sensory modalities, especially a match between a user's physical movement and movement in the virtual world, such as immediate visual change when the head moves or virtual reflection of walking or hand movement.
[4] Surrounding, as a quality of immersion, is the extent to which cues are panoramic, such as the extent of visual field of view or the extent of auditory source perception, and a wide field of view produces a more surrounding experience than a narrow field of view.
[5] Vivid, as a quality of immersion, refers to the amount of energy stimulated within a particular sensory modality and is related to factors such as resolution, lighting, frame rate, and audio bit rate, with higher resolution or audio bit rate improving visual or auditory perception and making immersion more vivid.
[6] Interactivity, as a quality of immersion, is the user's capability to make changes to the virtual world, receive responses from virtual entities to user actions, and influence future events, not merely one-way interaction.
[7] Plot-informing, as a quality of immersion, means the experience is a scripted story, and the more the user can understand, comprehend, or predict the consequences of actions and the overall story, including its consistent portrayal, dynamic unfolding, and behavior of the world and its entities, the more plot-informing the experience is.
[8] In virtual reality (VR), immersion is the technological issue and presence is the psychological issue.

Facts:
[1] Immersion is an objective and quantifiable description of what a particular system can provide or does provide, and that description can be measured or comprehended.
[2] Presence is a state of consciousness or psychological sense of being in the virtual environment that exists inside the user's mind, has no direct manifestation, is difficult to measure objectively, and therefore requires the user's subjective experience to be taken into account.
[3] Presence can be a function of both the user's subjective experience and a system's immersion, that is the objective or technological experience, so immersion can aid an enhanced perception of presence and is capable of producing presence, but it does not ensure presence.
[4] Presence can be limited by immersion, and the greater the immersion a system or application provides, the greater the potential for a user to feel present in the virtual world, while the lesser the immersive technology provides, the lesser the presence.
[5] The overall goal of any virtual reality system is to create a high degree of presence, that is to make users feel that they are really in the virtual world and unable to distinguish the real world from the virtual world.
[6] Creating a high degree of presence in a virtual reality system requires the system to provide a high degree of immersion, and this requirement is a systemic issue.

Course Foundation for Virtual and Augmented Reality Systems. Lecture Cybersickness. Segment goal: Explain how field of view and type of content influence cybersickness.

Facts:
[1] Field of view (FOV) is a content-related factor in virtual reality (VR) that affects susceptibility to cybersickness (CS), and it is the extent to which the display in a VR headset captures the user's field of vision.
[2] A larger field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) captures a larger field of vision and generally results in greater immersion.
[3] Research has found that reducing the field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) can be an effective way to alleviate symptoms of cybersickness (CS).
[4] An excessively narrow field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) can decrease immersion and increase head movement to look for things in the environment, which may exacerbate or increase cybersickness (CS); finding the optimal FOV is crucial for creating a comfortable VR experience.
[5] The type of content is an important factor in cybersickness (CS), and action content, fast movements, and abrupt alterations in a virtual reality (VR) environment are found to induce more CS than neutral and static content.
[6] For users with a high preference for adrenaline sports or adventurous things, exposure to action content, fast movements, or abrupt alterations in a virtual reality (VR) environment may not lead to severe cybersickness (CS) compared with users who are not exposed to such sports or adventures, because they are already accustomed to such behavior and environments.
[7] The genre of a virtual environment affects cybersickness (CS), and content based on horror scenes is likely to induce more CS than pleasant general content.
[8] The geometry and terrain of a virtual environment affect cybersickness (CS); when a user travels over regular bumps and irregular terrain, CS is more likely than when the same travel occurs over flat terrain without bumpy rides.
[9] Weather conditions in a virtual environment affect the induction of cybersickness (CS); stormy conditions are more likely to cause higher CS than clear weather conditions.

[1] In virtual reality (VR), an external factor in cybersickness (CS) is a factor that is not subjective to a user's mental or physical condition, and hardware is one category of external factors.

[3] Display resolution is a hardware factor that reduces cybersickness (CS) up to a certain point; a study evaluating 1K, 2K, 3K, and 4K resolutions found a substantial reduction in CS induction from 1K to 2K, but no significant further reduction from 2K to 3K or from 3K to 4K.
[4] Latency in virtual reality (VR) is the time delay, or time gap, between a user's movement in the physical world and the corresponding change in the virtual world.
[5] In head-mounted display (HMD)-based virtual reality (VR), cybersickness (CS) increases with latency; the more latency there is, the more likely it is to induce cybersickness.
[6] Latency jitter is variability in latency, meaning that the time gap between a physical-world action and its virtual-world reflection changes from time to time.
[7] Latency jitter causes irregularities in the timing of data delivery and can lead to inconsistencies, discomfort, disorientation, and cybersickness (CS).
[8] Display type is a hardware factor that significantly influences the severity of cybersickness (CS), with users using head-mounted display (HMD)-based or virtual reality (VR) headset displays experiencing more CS than users using conventional monitors or non-immersive VR systems; in one study comparing stereoscopic three-dimensional (3D) videos on flat screens, panoramic screens, and VR headsets, VR headset users experienced more CS.
[9] Users with higher-end head-mounted displays (HMDs) experience less cybersickness (CS) than users with lower-end HMDs, a difference related to display qualities such as resolution, brightness, clarity, and contrast.
[10] In virtual reality (VR), the type of input method used, such as hand controllers, treadmills, and motion sensors, can influence the level of cybersickness (CS).
[11] In virtual reality (VR), motion controllers such as steering with handlebars may cause more cybersickness (CS) than non-motion controls such as a joystick, and a gamepad controller causes less cybersickness than a hand controller.

We need analyze facts and concepts. Course XR, lecture Cybersickness. Segment goal: describe input-process-output framework for measuring cybersickness and questionnaire-based inputs used for it.

Facts:
[1] Measurement techniques for cybersickness (CS) rely on three components: the input provided for measurement, the measurement technique itself, and the output generated.
[2] Inputs for measuring cybersickness (CS) can be questionnaire-based, physiological and biometric information, behavioral information, and content-based information.
[3] The measurement technique or evaluation process for cybersickness (CS) can be manual, automated, machine learning-based, or real-time evaluation while the experience is taking place.
[4] The output of cybersickness (CS) measurement can be binary classes, multiple classes, or a sickness score that is a number.
[5] Questionnaire-based input for measuring cybersickness (CS) is a common method that uses self-report questionnaires or scales, generally in the form of ratings, to rate users' discomfort or disorientation on a numerical scale.
[6] Questionnaire-based cybersickness (CS) scales are easy to administer and help researchers or practitioners better understand the causes of cybersickness and identify potential interventions.
[7] Questionnaire-based cybersickness (CS) scales are typically administered before or after an experience, can also be administered during the experience, with before and after being the most common timing and during being occasional.
[8] The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) is one of the most extensively used questionnaires for measuring cybersickness (CS).
[9] The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) contains 16 items divided into three subscales: the oculomotor subscale, the disorientation subscale, and the nausea subscale.
[10] In the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ), participants rate the intensity of individual symptoms belonging to the oculomotor, disorientation, and nausea subscales on a scale from 0 to 3, where a higher score denotes more severe symptoms.
[11] The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) was not originally designed for virtual reality (VR) but was adapted for use in the context of virtual reality.
[12] Questionnaires specifically designed for virtual reality (VR) include the Virtual Reality Sickness Questionnaire (VRSQ) and the Cyber Sickness Questionnaire (CSQ), which is good for evaluating virtual reality experiences with head-mounted displays (HMDs).
[13] Shorter and more concise questionnaires used to assess specific conditions include the Misery Scale (MIS) and the Fast Motion Sickness Scale (FMS).
[14] Questionnaires used to measure susceptibility to cybersickness (CS) include the Motion History Questionnaire (MHQ), the Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (MS-SQ), and the Visually Induced Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (VIMS or VIMS-SQ).
[15] Questionnaires commonly used to assess overall discomfort include the Nausea Scale and the Motion Sickness Assessment Questionnaire (MSAQ).

[1] Non-hand input techniques in virtual reality (VR) consist of head tracking, eye tracking, full-body tracking, and sound-based tracking.
[2] Full-body tracking is a non-hand input method in virtual reality (VR) that tracks full-body movement, more than the head, hands, and eyes.
[3] Full-body tracking can add to the illusion of self-embodiment and social presence in a virtual world because its output can show the user a fuller representation of themselves.
[4] There are two broad approaches to full-body tracking: a motion capture suit (MOCAP) and camera-based tracking.
[5] In a motion capture suit (MOCAP) approach to full-body tracking, sensors in the suit capture and transmit raw movement data, which are combined and converted into full-body position and movement; for example, the Perception Neuron suit uses straps with inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors on the legs, hands, arms, and head.
[6] In camera-based full-body tracking, multiple surrounding cameras observe an actor wearing a suit with fiducial markers, typically reflective markers, and infer the actor's overall body movement from the markers' movement; OptiTrack and Microsoft Kinect are examples of such camera-based full-body tracking systems.
[7] Sound-based tracking is a non-hand input technique in virtual reality (VR) that captures voice, speech, and non-speech sound for interaction using simple microphones or microphone arrays, which are sets of microphones that capture sound in a 360-degree environment.

Course Foundation for VR/AR systems. Segment goal: processing/computer component of VR system, selection factors, roles of GPU, CPU, RAM.

Facts:
[1] In a virtual reality (VR) system, the processing part or computer is a device that processes data from input sensors and, based on that processing, activates or actuates output devices.
[2] The processing element or computer in a virtual reality (VR) system may be a standard personal computer (PC), a high-end workstation with a high-quality graphics processing unit (GPU), a distributed computer system interconnected through a high-speed communication network, or a smartphone, and its selection depends on the application, the target users, the assumed input and output devices and their availability, and the required level of immersion.
[3] The major components of a computer used as the processing element in a virtual reality (VR) system are the graphics processing unit (GPU), the central processing unit (CPU), and random access memory (RAM).
[4] A graphics processing unit (GPU) is used to speed up the rendering process because of its inherent parallel processing abilities and the inherent parallelism in the rendering process, and it is therefore very useful for rendering complex graphics and complex scenes that are part of realistic virtual reality (VR) experiences.
[5] Multi-GPU-enabled systems are typically used for building virtual reality (VR) applications, and a good-quality graphics processing unit (GPU)-enabled graphics card or GPU-enabled environment is preferable, especially for rendering.
[6] In virtual reality (VR) processing, multicore processors greatly increase computational capacity compared with non-multicore or unicore processors, and nowadays processors are multicore by default.
[7] Modern central processing unit (CPU) processors are quite powerful, but they have many other tasks to do, so a CPU-only virtual reality (VR) processing system with minimal graphics processing unit (GPU) support can have performance issues, and GPU support is preferable.
[8] An extended reality (XR) engine is middleware required to support, develop, and render virtual reality (VR) experiences.

[1] Output devices for virtual reality (VR) experience include visual displays, audio output, haptics, motion platforms and treadmills, and other sensory outputs that stimulate the taste and smell sensory organs, namely the tongue and nose.
[2] Other sensory output systems for taste and smell in virtual reality (VR) are premature, not widely used, available, or popular, and are mostly confined to highly specialized environments or research domains.
[3] Visual displays are displays meant to stimulate the visual sense, that is the eyes.
[4] The three broad types of visual displays are head-mounted displays (HMDs), which are wearable and mobile, world-fixed displays, which are not wearable and are stationary, and regular displays, which are mobile or can be stationary.
[5] Although head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be used as input to track head motion, their primary use is as a display device.
[6] A head-mounted display (HMD) is a sophisticated piece of equipment that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components within its package.
[7] A head-mounted display (HMD) places images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens, with one screen providing monoscopic viewing and two screens providing stereoscopic viewing, and stereoscopic HMDs are more common than monoscopic HMDs.
[8] Head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be further categorized into three types: non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through.
[9] Non-see-through HMDs are typically used in virtual reality (VR), optical see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented reality (AR), and video see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented virtuality, in which real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment.
[10] A world-fixed display renders graphics onto a surface or screen that is fixed and does not move with the user's head; the display is not moving, while the user can move within a physical space.
[11] World-fixed displays range from standard monitors to displays that completely surround the user, typically called a cave.
[12] The fish tank display, developed in 1993, is an early world-fixed virtual reality (VR) display that uses a fixed cathode-ray tube (CRT) monitor as the output and an optical head tracker and a haptic device as inputs, so that the stereo perspective view of a 3D scene changes as the user's head moves.
[13] A more recent world-fixed display example is the surround screen, or cave system, which typically has three to six large screens around the user for visual immersion and is usually driven by a single or group of powerful graphics engines and requires elaborate tracking of the user's movements.
[14] Regular displays, which can be mobile or stationary, refer to common tablets or smartphones, are not specialized, are typically relevant for non-immersive virtual reality (VR), and are mostly used for augmented reality (AR).

[6] Self-grounded haptic devices are worn or held by the user and move with the user, with handheld controllers as examples, whereas world-grounded haptic devices are physically attached to the real world, cannot be moved, and can provide the sense of fully solid objects that do not move.
[7] Motion platforms are hardware output devices that move the entire body to produce a sense of physical motion and gravity, conveying a sense of orientation, vibration, acceleration, and jerks.
[8] Use of motion platforms may result in motion sickness, which can be reduced by decreasing the conflict between visual motion and the perceived motion in the real world.
[9] Motion platforms can be active, meaning they are controlled by computer simulation, or passive, meaning they are controlled by the user with no direct computer control, and passive platforms are likely to result in less motion sickness than active platforms.
[10] Treadmills are output devices that provide the sense of walking or running while staying in one place by providing different sorts of input to the feet or legs.

[6] Inside-out tracking is a tracking type in which the cameras or other sensors required for tracking are located within the device used for the experience, such as the head-mounted display (HMD) in virtual reality (VR), which is more common, so no other external devices are needed.

Facts:
[1] Registration is the step that finds the initial pose or initial orientation of the sensor or user and sets the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds, represented as theta at t = 0.
[2] A simplifying assumption for understanding registration is that the direction the headset is facing when the tracking system is turned on is taken as the initial orientation, with the initial alignment set to the forward direction.
[3] Registration can be aided by fiducial markers, reflectors, or tags; it can also be performed without them using computer vision techniques, and the process is simpler when such aids are present.
[4] Integration is the stage that computes the current sensor orientation theta_t at time t = k delta_t by adding to the initial orientation estimated during registration, theta_0, the sum of calibrated angular velocity samples W_cal_i times the sampling interval delta_t over the elapsed samples; the sensor data stream usually arrives at regular discrete intervals, and k is an integer.
[5] A calibrated angular velocity sample W_cal_i is the angular velocity sample from a gyroscopic sensor at instant i, and it indicates a change in orientation equal to W_cal_i multiplied by the sampling interval delta_t.

[1] Spatial augmented reality (AR) devices are the third category of augmented reality devices, also known as room-scale augmented reality or tabletop augmented reality, and they typically use projectors to display graphical information on physical objects; unlike headsets, glasses, or handheld devices, they overlay digital content on physical objects in the real world rather than on the user's view of the real world.
[2] A defining feature of spatial augmented reality (AR) devices is that their display element is not tied to or held by the user, unlike headsets, glasses, or handheld devices, and they can provide more natural and intuitive interfaces than these other device categories.
[3] Spatial augmented reality (AR) devices allow multiple users to interact simultaneously with digital content augmented onto a physical object, whereas with headsets, glasses, or handheld devices each user interacts only with the content on that user's own device and others cannot interact with it.
[4] Major application areas for spatial augmented reality (AR) devices and systems include education, art and design, medical training, industrial applications, museums and exhibits, and entertainment.
[5] The fundamental principle of a spatial augmented reality (AR) system is that it augments the physical environment by adding virtual objects that seem to coexist in the same space as real objects, so the digitally augmented content appears to coexist with the physical space surrounding the user.
[6] Implementing a spatial augmented reality (AR) system requires understanding the geometry and lighting conditions of the physical environment for seamless mixing, which can be achieved using advanced depth sensors or computer vision techniques typically included in the system.
[7] Projection-based augmented reality (AR) systems and spatial augmented reality systems generally refer to similar ideas.
[8] Examples of spatial augmented reality (AR) systems discussed as major categories include interactive projectors, air sandboxes, projection keyboards, and projection mapping.
[9] An interactive projector is an example of a spatial augmented reality (AR) system that projects images or interfaces onto any surface, turning the surface into an interactive display; for example, a projector can project an interface onto a tabletop, making the tabletop an interactive display and an augmented reality experience, and Sony Xperia Touch is an example.
[10] An air sandbox is an example of a spatial augmented reality (AR) system that uses a projector and a sensor, such as a three-dimensional (3D) camera like Microsoft Kinect, to project a topographic map onto a physical box of sand and update the map in real time when users move the sand or gesture, allowing two to three users to interact simultaneously.
[11] A projection keyboard is an example of a spatial augmented reality (AR) system that projects a virtual keyboard onto a flat surface, converting that surface into an interactive keyboard, and it may use infrared sensors to detect finger positions, which is the more common way to handle key-press interaction.
[12] Projection mapping technology is a software-based application of spatial augmented reality (AR) in which software solutions such as TouchDesigner, MadMapper, or HeavyM are used with standard projectors to create complex projections onto three-dimensional (3D) space without a surface, for example projecting a map or a model of the Earth in air.
[13] Projection mapping displays can be interacted with by rotating, pinching, zooming in, or zooming out.
[14] Projection mapping is commonly used in entertainment and gaming industries.

Facts:
[1] Inertial trackers are self-contained sensors that measure rate of change in object orientation, translation velocity, or acceleration, and they measure only changes rather than absolute values.
[2] Inertial trackers are typically based on microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) and are part of the device that the user is using, for example most smartphones and head-mounted displays (HMDs) nowadays, so they have no range limitation and can be readily used for tracking.
[3] Hybrid software-level sensors can be designed using the primary inertial sensors (a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer) and can be part of the device.
[4] Basic types of tracking sensors typically used include electromechanical, electromagnetic, inertial, three-dimensional (3D) structure sensing, and light-based sensing.
[5] Sensing approaches that do not directly fit into the basic tracking sensor categories include acoustic sensing and the global positioning system (GPS).
[6] The global positioning system (GPS) is a positional tracking device that is particularly useful in outdoor environments.
[7] The global positioning system (GPS) generally offers low accuracy, particularly in indoor environments, and allows only positional tracking.
[8] Real time kinematic (RTK) technology can be used with a basic global positioning system (GPS) sensor to improve detection accuracy by using global positioning system signal carrier waves for measurement, providing further accuracy than the basic global positioning system.
[9] The global positioning system (GPS) is typically utilized when accurate position registration is not important, when an approximation is good enough, or as part of a hybrid tracking system with other tracking systems.

[1] The virtual world generator (VWG) is an abstraction of the whole virtual reality (VR) software system, treated as a black box whose internal operation is not considered.
[2] The virtual world generator (VWG) receives input from low-level systems such as a head tracker that estimates the user's head position and orientation, a keyboard, a mouse, and a game controller, and other input devices, and simultaneous input events are arranged in a queue so that they can be processed systematically.
[3] The virtual world generator (VWG) must maintain an internal reality that appears real to the user, convert incoming input into output so that renderers can extract information and calculate outputs for their displays, and keep output devices synchronized with the input data to maintain an input-output match.
[4] The virtual world generator (VWG) can use several output renderers, including a visual renderer that generates a visual display, an aural renderer that generates an aural display sensed by the ears, and a haptic renderer that generates a haptic display sensed by the skin, along with other possible renderers.
[5] A completely synthetic virtual world requires defining a triangular mesh in a three-dimensional space and maintaining material and physical surface properties that indicate how the surfaces interact with light, sound, and forces.
[6] Computer graphics addresses computer-generated images from synthetic models, and the software that helps a developer build a virtual reality (VR) experience should support computer-graphics operations.
[7] A virtual world can also be a recorded physical world, made realistic by capturing the real world with cameras and using computer-vision and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) techniques, so virtual reality (VR) software may require support for SLAM or computer-vision techniques.
[8] One possibility for creating a virtual world is texture mapping, in which camera images of a real object are mapped onto a synthetic object; this is a common computer-graphics operation that virtual reality (VR) software should ideally support.

Facts:
[1] Matched motion in virtual reality (VR) is the maintenance of correspondence between a user's motions in the real world and the virtual world.
[2] A matched zone is a place where the real world and the virtual world perfectly align; it corresponds to the safe real-world region where a user's physical movement is restricted, although the virtual world is not similarly confined, and movement within that region is translated to movement in other parts of the virtual world.
[3] In an immersive virtual reality (VR) application that is not carefully implemented, an obstacle mismatch can occur when a virtual obstacle blocks the user without a corresponding physical obstacle in the matched zone, or when a physical obstacle exists in the matched zone without a corresponding virtual obstacle.
[4] In virtual reality (VR), the real-world motions reflected in the virtual world vary among virtual reality experiences: head motions must be matched so the visual renderer uses the correct viewpoint, and other body parts require tracking and matched motion when the user needs hand-eye coordination or looks at those body parts during the experience.
[5] Virtual reality (VR) software should include developer support for resolving matched-motion challenges, such as deciding which real-world motions to reflect and creating a correspondence between a user's physical motion in the matched zone and a different virtual motion.
[6] User locomotion in virtual reality (VR), which is closely related to matched motion, is moving oneself in the virtual world while one's physical motion in the real world is not matched; it is motivated because users often want to move well outside the matched zone.
[7] Teleportation in virtual reality (VR) is a locomotion operation in which a user can pull up a menu, point to a desired virtual location, and be sent to that location without making any physical movement.
[8] A popular option for user locomotion in virtual reality (VR) is operating a game controller, mouse, or keyboard so the user's avatar can walk, run, jump, swim, climb, board a vehicle, and operate its controls while the user remains seated; the vehicle option is a vehicle metaphor.
[9] Virtual reality (VR) locomotion operations that let the user avoid physical movement may lead to cyber sickness, which increases with exposure duration and other factors.
[10] Support for user locomotion, including different sorts of locomotion so that cyber sickness can be addressed, should be part of virtual reality (VR) software.

Course: Foundation for VR/AR. Segment: VR Software. Goal compare building VR experience from SDKs vs ready-made VWG.

Facts:
[1] To build a virtual reality (VR) experience, a developer can either build a virtual world generator (VWG) from scratch using a basic software development kit (SDK) for a specific headset, device, or platform, or use a ready-made virtual world generator (VWG) customized by choosing menu options and writing high-level scripts.
[2] A basic software development kit (SDK) for a headset, device, or platform is typically expected to provide basic drivers to drive the hardware, interfaces or application programming interfaces (APIs) to access tracking data, and application programming interfaces (APIs) to make calls to graphical rendering libraries; in a virtual world generator (VWG), basic drivers and tracking cover some aspects and rendering covers other aspects, but not every aspect of locomotion or matched motion, physics, or networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience is typically taken care of by the software development kit (SDK).
[3] When building a virtual world generator (VWG) from a basic software development kit (SDK), the developer must build, at the very least, the physics support of the virtual world from scratch, handling problems such as movement of an avatar, collision detection, occurrence of collision and the response to it, lighting models, and audio support; sometimes collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience support is also required.
[4] Using a basic software development kit (SDK) to build a virtual world generator (VWG) from scratch gives the developer maximum control and the ability to optimize performance because the developer can choose and implement the algorithms for physics support according to performance, rather than being forced to use whatever comes with a package.
[5] Using a basic software development kit (SDK) to build a virtual world generator (VWG) from scratch imposes a difficult implementation burden and requires a lot of effort to understand and implement the overall system from scratch.
[6] OpenSimulator and Unity3D can provide ready-made virtual world generator (VWG) support; OpenSimulator is an open-source alternative to Second Life designed to support developers in building a virtual society of avatars, and Unity3D is a popular game engine adapted to work for virtual reality (VR).
[7] A ready-made virtual world generator (VWG) or higher-level engine makes it easy for developers to create a virtual reality (VR) experience in little time because it comes with supports, including support for collisions or physics, so the developer does not have to build from scratch.
[8] A ready-made virtual world generator (VWG) or engine is harder to use for highly original experiences not imagined by the engine builder because it comes with its own function supports and algorithm implementations that the developer must use, which restricts the developer, although it reduces effort.

[1] Augmented Reality (AR) software tools can be categorized by developer skill, target application platform (desktop AR applications or mobile AR applications), or tracking technology (computer vision (CV)-based tracking or other sensors such as Global Positioning System (GPS) sensors).

[3] The skill requirements for the four skill-based Augmented Reality (AR) software tool categories are: low-level software libraries or frameworks require strong programming or coding ability and understanding of how to call the library functions; rapid prototyping tools require some programming ability, lower than for low-level tools, and may require design prototyping skills; plugins require skill with the original developer tool with which the plugin is used; and standalone AR authoring tools assume no programming ability and can be used without any knowledge.
[4] Examples of Augmented Reality (AR) software tools for each skill-based category are: AR Toolkit, OSG Art, StudiersTube, and MXR Toolkit for low-level software libraries or frameworks; FLAR Manager and OpenFrameworks for rapid prototyping tools; AR media plugins, Vuforia, MetaIO Unity plugins, and Dart for plugins for existing developer tools; and BuildAR, MetaIO Creator, and Wikitude for standalone AR authoring tools.

[1] Plugins to existing tools are a category of augmented reality (AR) software in which a plugin is added to an existing interactive two-dimensional (2D) or three-dimensional (3D) content authoring tool that may not itself support AR content or system development, and the plugin adds AR-specific functions such as tracking, visualization, and 3D registration of digital content over the real-world view, while relying on the main authoring tool for content authoring.
[2] Plugins to existing tools provide an easy and quick method for developing augmented reality (AR) applications when the developer already knows the host authoring tool, because the developer can rely on knowledge of the original tool and only needs to understand the plugin, reducing the required understanding of the system; if the developer does not know the authoring tool, the approach makes no sense because everything must be learned from scratch.
[3] Many interactive three-dimensional (3D) graphics authoring tools, including Unity, Vizard, and Lumion, are used to create interactive 3D applications, and most of these tools have plugins for augmented reality (AR) visualization; Unity has the widest range of available solutions for AR visualization.
[4] The augmented reality (AR) Toolkit for Unity from the AR Tool Works is an example of an AR plugin for Unity that provides marker-based tracking, image-based or computer-vision-based tracking, and AR visualization support.
[5] Vuforia is a tracking library that has an augmented reality (AR) plugin that works with Unity three-dimensional (3D) and can be used to create AR applications, particularly mobile AR applications for iOS and Android platforms.
[6] Limitations of using plugins to add augmented reality (AR) support to existing content authoring tools are that user interface and interaction design can be limited to what the underlying authoring tool provides, software and hardware configuration depends on that tool, and content produced with the authoring tool usually becomes dependent on proprietary player software in most cases.
[7] A way to resolve the limitations of higher-level augmented reality (AR) tools or plugins is to use low-level software development tools, such as software libraries, and build the system from scratch rather than depending on a third-party tool, an approach that applies to any higher-level tool.

Course title: Foundation for Virtual and Augmented Reality Systems. Lecture: XR as Interactive Systems. Segment goal: Explain how novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization can guide interactive-system design without always requiring field studies.

Facts:
[1] Empirical or field studies of user behavior are typically needed to understand who the users of an interactive system are and how they behave, but they are time-consuming, laborious, and require elaborate setup and planning, so interactive-system designers can rely on the novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization instead of always starting with field studies.
[2] A three-class classification of interactive-system users consists of novice users, who use the system for the first time, intermittent users, who use it occasionally, and expert users, who use it regularly over a long period of time.
[3] In the novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization, an expert user is not a technology expert but a person who is an expert in using the system and can use it efficiently.
[4] The novice, intermittent, and expert user classes provide a starting point for understanding users and making interactive-system design decisions when designers assume their potential users belong to one of these classes, because users in different classes are likely to behave differently and designers can broadly understand the behavior of each class.
[5] A word processing or similar processing application can provide multiple options, such as a hotkey combination and a menu option, for the same task to cater to different user groups.
[6] For saving a file, the menu option takes longer than the hotkey combination but is suitable for novice first-time users because remembering hotkey combinations is generally difficult for them, while the hotkey combination may be a better alternative for intermittent users and is always preferable for expert users.
[7] The novice, intermittent, and expert categorization is only one broad way of classifying users; more fine-grained categorizations are possible, and better categorizations can be based on empirical studies of users, but the broad novice, intermittent, and expert categorization is useful when the design process starts.

[1] Field of view (FOV) is the view frustum, that is, the region visible to the human eye, and it is an angular measure of what can be seen at a single point in time.
[2] The human eye has an approximately 180-degree horizontal field of view (FOV) and a 150-degree vertical field of view, and within the 180-degree horizontal range a person sees things using both central and peripheral vision.
[3] In binocular vision, when both eyes focus on infinity, both eyes see the same image over a common region of about 120 degrees, while areas outside this region are seen only by the left eye or only by the right eye.
[4] Binocular vision enhances depth perception and helps a person understand the relationship between objects in three-dimensional (3D) space.
[5] Stereoscopy is the process in which two eyes view two images simultaneously, the left eye processes the left image, the right eye processes the right image, and there is a common part seen by both eyes while some parts are seen by only one eye.
[6] When the left and right two-dimensional (2D) images are processed simultaneously, the processing generates a three-dimensional (3D) view of the objects, so stereoscopic vision, which is aided by binocular vision, helps a person perceive three-dimensional objects.

[1] The human eye contains a cornea that acts as a powerful lens with fixed focal depth, a natural lens with variable focal depth, and a non-planar retina that is the image surface where light falls and is converted by photoreceptors into neural pulses transmitted to the brain through optical nerves.

[3] The interior of the human eye is liquid, so after transmission through the lens light passes through liquid, whereas in an artificially created lens setup light passes through air after the lens.
[4] In the human eye, a ray of light passes through five media before hitting the retina—air with refractive index 1.009, cornea with 1.376, aqueous fluid with 1.336, natural lens with 1.413, and vitreous fluid with 1.337—and each medium has its own refractive index.
[5] Because the outer diameter of the human eyeball is approximately 24 millimeters, a single lens of at least 40 diopters would be required to converge parallel rays onto the center of the retina.
[6] The human eye effectively contains two convex lenses, the cornea with optical power of approximately 40 diopters and the natural lens with approximately 20 diopters, so their combined optical power is about 60 diopters, which is sufficient to focus images of faraway objects onto the retina.
[7] A virtual reality (VR) headset places a screen very close to the eyes to fill the view and uses a convex lens, functioning like reading glasses, to focus the screen's light on the retina, after which normal eye operation takes over.
[8] For the best experience, the screen in a virtual reality (VR) headset is placed at the focal length of its engineered lens, so that the screen appears to the user as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance.
[9] In a virtual reality (VR) headset, even though the screen appears as a virtual image, a real image is nevertheless formed on the retina, and a person does not perceive the world unless real images are formed on the retina.

[3] Stevens' power law is a result from psychophysics that characterizes the relationship between the magnitude of a physical stimulus and its perceived magnitude by the equation P = C M^x, where M is the magnitude or intensity of the original stimulus, P is the perceived magnitude, x is the exponent that relates actual magnitude to perceived magnitude, and C is a constant that depends on units.
[4] The just noticeable difference (JND) is a result from psychophysics that specifies the amount of change in a stimulus that is required for subjects to perceive it as changed in at least 50 percent of trials.
[5] Weber's law captures the just noticeable difference (JND), the change in magnitude that is noticeable, by representing it as delta M divided by M equals C, where M is the magnitude or intensity of the stimulus, delta M is the just noticeable difference, and C is a constant; equivalently, delta M equals M times C.
[6] Weber's law and Stevens' power law are laws from psychophysics that also apply to psychoacoustics, or auditory perception, when physical stimuli are replaced by acoustic stimuli.
[7] For the perceived loudness of a 3000 hertz (Hz) pure tone, the Stevens' power law exponent x is 0.67, so a much higher pressure level is perceived as only a bit louder because the exponent is less than 1.
[8] For a change in a stimulus to be perceived, it must be above the just noticeable difference (JND); for it not to be perceived, it must be within or below the JND.

Course: Foundation for VR/AR Systems, lecture Auditory Sense & Immersive Experience. Segment goal: Explain how binaural localization cues and HRTF are used to render localized binaural sound in XR.

Facts:
[1] Sound localization cues are either monaural, involving a single ear, or binaural, involving both ears.
[2] Interaural level difference (ILD) is a binaural sound localization cue that is the difference in sound magnitude heard by each ear, with the ear without obstruction receiving a stronger sound, and the difference can indicate the direction from which the sound is coming.
[3] An acoustic shadow occurs when a sound wave does not reach one ear, caused by an object in front of the sound source or by the position of the head.
[4] Interaural time difference is a binaural sound localization cue from different sound arrival times at the ears; in an average human head, the ears are 21.5 centimeters apart, sound travels that distance in about 0.6 milliseconds, and this small time difference can be used to locate the source.
[5] The auditory component of an extended reality (XR) system should ideally be non-stationary, moving with the user, and interactive, dependent on the listener's actions.
[6] Head-related transfer functions (HRTF) model how a listener receives sound from a location in space, and this model is relevant for dealing with sound in any system, including extended reality (XR) systems.
[7] Head-related transfer functions (HRTF) depend on the size and shape of the head, ears, and ear canal, and every person has a unique HRTF.
[8] Because every person has a unique head-related transfer function (HRTF), it is impractical to determine individual users' HRTFs when building a system, so an HRTF for an average listener is developed and used.

Facts:
[1] A design space is the set of all possible designs, and when n distinct objects are placed on a screen without repetition, the typical size of the design space is n factorial, with the number of arrangements increasing if repetition is allowed.
[2] A calendar application has a fixed and large number of elements to be displayed, such as month names, dates, and possibly the year, so it has a very large design space.
[3] In a calendar application, many possible designs may be invalid because dates must be ordered in a particular way, but in most practical systems a reasonably significant number of valid design choices can remain, such as 10, 15, or 20.
[4] A software development life cycle (SDLC) is a systematic approach that helps identify the best valid design choice in terms of usability, because intuition may not lead to the single best solution for everyone.

Facts:
[1] Touch sensation in extended reality (XR) can be provided by engineered devices, and the most popular form is force feedback, typically in the form of vibrations, provided by force feedback devices such as a force feedback mouse, smart gloves, and body suits, which are common in many XR systems, particularly virtual reality (VR) systems.
[2] The KGS dot view model DV-2 is a haptic pin array with a matrix of pins that a computer controls, and the pins are forced upward, according to signals generated for objects in the virtual world, to simulate the texture of an object surface when the user's fingertip scans across it.
[3] Controlling a haptic pin array precisely enough to give a realistic feeling of a textured surface is generally difficult and challenging.
[4] Real-world objects whose virtual avatars appear in a virtual world and that are used in place of computer-controlled haptic devices to provide feedback to the user's somatosensory system are sometimes called tangible user interfaces.
[5] To give the feeling of touching a real object surface in a virtual world, using real objects to provide touch feedback is generally considered less challenging than creating a computer-controlled haptic device.
[6] The basic idea for implementing tangible user interfaces is to create the experience by aligning the real world and the virtual world.
[7] A see-through display such as Microsoft HoloLens, which is typically good for mixed reality or augmented reality, enables users to see and interact with the physical world around them, and it adds virtual objects to the real world or visually enhances real objects.
[8] In a see-through display such as Microsoft HoloLens, the computer uses wearable device sensors to detect which real object the user is dealing with and can change the view of that object or add virtual objects to the real world.

Facts:
[1] Haptic perception is a major part of somatosensory perception, and it is the perception of the overall geometric shape of objects as part of touch perception.
[2] Haptic exploration is the handling or manipulation of geometric objects that is used to infer the overall geometric shape of the object.
[3] Haptic perception can be thought of at different levels: receptors in the skin receive input from the real world and process the information to perceive something through touch, while higher-level perception requires object manipulations that are called haptic explorations.
[4] The six types of haptic exploration, each needed for a different object property perception, are lateral motion for texture perception, pressure for hardness perception, enclosure for global shape or volume perception, static contact for temperature perception, unsupported holding for weight perception, and contour following for local shape perception.
[5] Each haptic exploration used to perceive different properties of objects involves different kinds of receptors and a combination of spatial and temporal information.
[6] The overall goal of haptic exploration is to integrate somatosensory signals from in-hand manipulation of an object so that a geometric mental model of the object is learned in terms of properties such as shape, size, weight and hardness.
[7] Haptic perception is important for creating a mental model of the surrounding world, and because mental model creation is an essential part of an immersive experience, haptic perception can improve an immersive experience.
[8] Haptic perception and haptic exploration offer an extra dimension to virtual reality (VR) by letting users feel the virtual environment through the sense of touch, which gives users a better feeling of the virtual world and helps them feel truly immersed in the virtual world, and because immersion in the real world also involves haptic exploration, adding haptic exploration to a virtual world increases the immersive experience.
[9] In a virtual desert walking example, visual and auditory perception alone may not give a complete picture of the haptic touch perception of feeling sand glide under the feet, and adding haptic exploration support through proper hardware and software makes the experience far better than an experience using only visual or auditory senses.

[1] The digital heritage preservation system for Majuli island has two components: preservation, which produces the content of the virtual tour, and experiencing the heritage through immersive virtual tours, which allow users to explore the island virtually.
[2] Majuli island's distinct tribal cultures are present in tribal villages that dot the landscape, its three major tribes are Mishing, Deori, and Sonowal Kacharis, each of which is supposed to have a distinct tangible and intangible cultural identity, and the villages' unique traditions and customs should be reproduced in a virtual tour.
[3] The intangible cultural heritage of Majuli island includes festivals and rituals that celebrate cultural diversity throughout the year, including the traditional Bihu, the harvest festival of Assam, which takes place on the island with colorful dances, traditional music, and feasts, and the festivals Kati Bihu, Raas Leela, Ali Ai Ligang, and Bhogali Bihu; their timings and forms should be known so that similar experiences can be reproduced in the virtual world.
[4] The Satras (Vaishnavite monasteries or sattras) on Majuli island are part of both tangible and intangible heritage, are the heart of the island's cultural landscape, and are centers of religious significance and cultural vitality.
[5] The intangible cultural heritage of Majuli island includes the Mati Akhara dance and the Khol musical instrument, with the Khol being played while the dance takes place, and these elements should be captured and reproduced in a virtual space.
[6] The traditional crafts of Majuli island residents include pottery, mask making, silk production, and boat building; these crafts are part of professional and daily life, serve as links to tangible and intangible heritage passed down through generations, and lead to trading with the outside world, so they should be captured.

Facts:
[1] The five stages of contextual inquiry are plan, initiate, execute, close, and reflect, in that order, and they provide a systematic way of carrying out the inquiry process.
[2] The plan stage of contextual inquiry involves identifying the goals of observation, gathering knowledge about the task domain, planning arrangements for recording observations, identifying the users and the date, time, and place of the observation, and, as a helpful practice, scripting and rehearsing the procedure.
[3] The initiate stage of contextual inquiry involves obtaining all necessary permissions from relevant authorities before observing employees in their workplace and opening communication with end users to remove anxieties that the observation may lead to something bad for them, so that they behave naturally.
[4] The execute stage of contextual inquiry is the stage in which the actual inquiry takes place, through performing observations and recording data.
[5] The close stage of contextual inquiry ideally involves formally closing by sending thank-you notes or a message of gratitude to the users and possibly the authorities, because such users may be useful for future activities such as usability testing.
[6] The reflect stage of contextual inquiry is the stage in which the observer or experimental team analyzes the data collected during the execute stage and identifies the design goals.
[7] The affinity diagram method is a technique used in the reflect stage of contextual inquiry to arrange the collected data so that patterns can be found more easily, leading to the design specification of the design goals.

Facts:
[1] The affinity diagram method is a method for analyzing data collected through contextual inquiry, and it consists of five steps: generate ideas, display ideas, sort ideas into groups, create a header or name for each group, and draw the finished diagram.
[2] In the affinity diagram method, the generated ideas are the observers' final notes from contextual inquiry, possibly refined in later processing, and displaying the ideas means putting those notes together in a place such as a wall or a board.
[3] Sorting ideas into groups in the affinity diagram method is done to find patterns among ideas that may look random, by moving similar ideas into the same group so that meaningful conclusions can be drawn.
[4] In the affinity diagram method, a group header is a name or identifier assigned to a group after the ideas have been sorted, and it refers to the pattern that binds the ideas within that group; the header is not present in the initial ideas.
[5] In the class note-taking application example, the 19 affinity-diagram ideas are organized into six groups with the headers navigation in notebook, media content, navigation in notes, note organization, text formatting, and storage and privacy, containing 3, 5, 2, 2, 4, and 3 ideas respectively.
[6] After the finished affinity diagram is drawn, reflection means deciding what to do with the data and formulating a set of design recommendations based on the data.
[7] Design recommendations or guidelines derived from contextual inquiry are informed design choices because they are produced by analyzing the collected inquiry data, whereas guidelines created without contextual inquiry are uninformed design choices that do not ensure that users' needs and expectations are taken into account.
[8] A design recommendation such as providing an erase-content facility in the class note-taking application for correcting mistakes is a requirement, not a prescription for implementation; it states what must be done to make the system usable, and it does not specify how to implement it.

COURSE TITLE Foundation for Virtual and Augmented Reality Systems, etc. Lecture usability requirement gathering and specification. Segment goal: Describe how usability requirements can be converted into functional requirements and specified in an SRS hierarchy.
FACTS:
[1] A functional requirement (FR) is a formally specifiable requirement that is easy to convert into code because it specifies a system feature as a black-box function with a well-defined input, a well-defined output, and an optional description of its purpose.
[2] Usability requirements, which are non-functional requirements (NFRs), can be converted into functional requirements (FRs) and added to the already obtained set of functional requirements, so that usability requirements are directly incorporated into the system through code and support code design.
[3] A software requirements specification (SRS) is the textual document that specifies all requirements of a system, both functional and non-functional, and it includes the formal specification of the functional requirements.
[4] In a software requirements specification (SRS), requirements are generally organized in a hierarchy with identifiers such as R1 for a top-level requirement and R1.1 for a sub-requirement, and each requirement identifier represents a function with a clearly defined input, a clearly defined output, and an optional description of what it does.
[5] The output of contextual inquiry is a group-wise organization of the notes taken during observation, and it can be used as design guidelines to ensure usability that cannot be immediately converted to code or, for some of them if not all, converted into functional requirements (FRs) that can be directly implemented as code.
[6] In the calendar app for college students example, the functional requirement R1 views takes a date as input and generates a specific view such as timetable, submission deadlines, or meeting list, with subrequirements R1.1 timetable view (date input, day timetable output), R1.2 deadline view (date input, submission deadlines output), and R1.3 meeting schedule (date input, list of meetings scheduled on the day output).

Course: XR, lecture System Design. Segment goal: Explain Shneiderman's first two golden rules, consistency and universal usability.
Facts:
[1] Shneiderman's first golden rule of system and interface design is to strive for consistency.
[2] The consistency required by Shneiderman's first golden rule has two types: internal consistency and external or environmental consistency.
[3] Internal consistency in system design means using the same elements and interactions for the same task across different parts of a design and different usage instances, rather than using separate objects, elements, or interactions.
[4] External or environmental consistency in system design means that the elements and interactions in a virtual world should closely match the user's real-world experience and knowledge, so that real-world knowledge transfers to the virtual world as closely as possible.
[5] Shneiderman's second golden rule is to design for universal usability, meaning a system should provide facilities for all user categories and support different user categories rather than only specific user categories.
[6] Menu-based options can be preferable to hotkey options for users who may not remember hotkey combinations because menu options rely on recognition rather than recall, and recall is a skilled task, whereas hotkeys such as Control plus S (Ctrl+S) are faster for users who do not want to use slower menu-based options.

Course: XR. Lecture System Design. Segment facts:
[1] Designing an immersive experience involves the design-prototype-evaluation cycle in order to incorporate user requirements.
[2] Interface and interaction design involves two issues: where or how to start the design process and how to express a design so that it can be brainstormed and refined, which means having a design language.
[3] Interface and interaction design requires creativity and imagination, and the design process can be started from creativity aided by intuition, expertise, experience, or domain knowledge, and/or from guidelines, often called checklists, heuristics, or thumb rules.
[4] Some design guidelines are generic, small in number, and cover broad high-level aspects of interactive systems; examples are Shneiderman's eight golden rules and Donald Norman's seven principles, both primarily intended for graphical user interfaces (GUIs) but applicable to other domains, with Norman's seven principles developed in the 1980s.
[5] Other design guidelines are more detailed and specific, generally large in number, and cover the micro details of a particular system or product; for example, Apple's human interface guidelines were originally developed for Apple's user interfaces.
[6] A design language is a specification of design, and there can be different languages for specifying a design; the language used to specify interface design is generally different from the language used to specify code design.
[7] A prototype can be considered a language for expressing interface and interaction design ideas.

Course Foundation for Virtual and Augmented Reality Systems, Lecture System Design, segment goal: Explain hand-based object selection techniques, including virtual hand, go-go, prism, and intent-driven selection.
Facts:
[1] A hand selection technique selects virtual objects in a virtual world with the user's hand by having the user directly reach out to virtually touch the object and trigger a grab; conventionally, selection with hand involves one hand, using a single finger or multiple fingers of one hand.
[2] Hand selection techniques for virtual objects include virtual hand, go-go, prism, and intent-driven selection.
[3] The virtual hand technique is the simplest and most intuitive hand selection technique, in which a visible virtual hand acts as an avatar of the user's physical hand and is tied to it through a one-to-one mapping of the physical hand's motion and orientation, typically implemented with three-dimensional (3D) tracked controllers, allowing natural hand movements.
[4] The virtual hand technique has a problem for selecting distant objects because moving the physical hand to reach them can require a long duration of physical hand movement, which can be tiring and annoying.
[5] The go-go technique is a virtual hand selection technique for distant objects that allows the user to interactively change the virtual arm length, the length of the virtual hand, uses one-to-one mapping when the target is close, and, as distance increases, maps smaller physical hand movements to larger and faster virtual hand movements, possibly exponentially, so that distant objects can be reached quickly.
[6] The go-go technique has a low-precision problem for selecting distant small objects because the virtual hand moves faster when the object is farther away, so a small physical hand movement can miss, bypass, or cross the target and is difficult to control.
[7] The prism technique is an improvement of the go-go technique that applies scaled-down motion to the virtual hand when the user's physical hand moves below a specified speed, and if the hand velocity is slower than a specified minimum velocity, the virtual hand remains still.
[8] For selecting distant objects, prism may provide a better solution than go-go because slowing or stopping the physical hand slows or stops the virtual hand, and the ability to stop the virtual hand when the physical hand stops is not present in go-go.
[9] Prism can result in a mismatch between the real and virtual hand positions because it does not use a one-to-one mapping, which may be counterintuitive.
[10] Intent-driven selection is a hand selection technique in which the user moves the virtual hand toward an object and positions virtual fingers, or uses the posture of virtual fingers, around the object to indicate the user's level of confidence in selecting that object.
[11] Intent-driven selection techniques typically use proximity spheres that encompass multiple objects at a larger distance and progressively reduce in size, depending on hand or finger postures, as the user moves closer to the intended object, refining the selection to a specific object.
[12] In hand selection techniques, go-go and prism are travel techniques, intent-driven selection is a grabbing technique, and intent-driven selection may be combined with a go-go or prism travel technique.

Segment facts:
[1] In any virtual experience, object interaction is broadly of two types: selection, which specifies one or more objects from a set of virtual objects in the virtual world, and manipulation, which interacts with a selected object to change its properties; the two types mostly have separate interaction techniques.
[2] For a given virtual experience, the kind of object selection technique that is suitable is determined by some of the most important parameters or variables that influence user performance while accomplishing the selection task, including the distance of the object to be selected from the current viewpoint or camera position, the direction of the object to be selected, the size of the object to be selected, the density of objects around the target object, and the number of targets to be selected, so that selection performance is maximized.
[3] Target occlusion can also be an important factor in selection performance: if a target is partly occluded by other surrounding objects, locating and selecting it is challenging and specialized techniques may be required, while fully occluded objects may also be selected, but the user must first be made aware of their presence, and specialized selection of fully occluded objects is a special case, with the majority of cases involving partially occluded or partially visible objects.
[4] Object selection techniques in a virtual world include selection with the hand, pointing-based selection, image plane selection, volume-based selection, and bimanual selection.

Task: List concepts in facts of lecture segment. Course XR. Segment goal: pointing-based object selection techniques, including ray casting, bend cast, depth ray.

Facts:
[1] Pointing-based selection is a selection technique in which the user operates a controller to extend a ray into the distance in the virtual world, sees the ray, and can select the first object intersected by the ray through a user-controlled trigger on the controller.
[2] Pointing for pointing-based selection can be done by hand pointing with a hand or handheld input device, by head pointing, in which a head-mounted display extends the ray from the head position and moves it with head movement without using the hand, or by eye-gaze pointing with an eye tracker.
[3] A virtual ray in pointing-based selection is a short line segment or an infinite line that can be attached to the virtual hand, head, or eye, with head position or eye gaze used when hand tracking is unavailable.
[4] Some pointing-based selection methods combine gaze pointing to estimate the target and hand pointing to trigger selection.
[5] Ray casting is the most basic way to extend a ray in pointing-based selection, in which the user points at objects with a virtual ray.
[6] In ray casting, selecting small distant objects is difficult and can require practice because the ray must be pointed precisely, and the difficulty increases when the small object is surrounded by other objects of similar, smaller, or larger size.
[7] Bend cast is an improvement over basic ray casting in which the system bends the ray toward the closest selectable object, detected by calculating the point-line distance from each selectable object, so the user need not point precisely, and a circular arc can provide visual feedback for the bending.
[8] Bend cast works best when only a few objects are near the ray's path, because with many nearby objects and similar distances the intended object may not be the closest, reintroducing the precision problem.
[9] Depth ray is an improvement over basic ray casting in which a user-controlled depth marker, positioned by moving the hand forward or backward, disambiguates multiple intersected objects and selects the object intersected by the pointing vector and closest to the marker.

[1] Indirect manipulation is a method sometimes used to manipulate virtual objects in which the user does not directly manipulate the virtual object using the physical hand, but instead manipulates other objects mapped to the virtual object, and those other objects in turn manipulate the virtual object.
[2] Three-dimensional (3D) widgets are a simple indirect manipulation technique in which controls are placed directly in the 3D scene with virtual objects, and manipulating a widget manipulates the associated virtual object.
[3] Each three-dimensional (3D) widget is typically responsible for only a small set of manipulation degrees of freedom, so a single widget may not be sufficient to manipulate all properties of a given object; instead, specified sets of degrees of freedom are manipulated using the individual widgets.
[4] Indirect proxies are an indirect manipulation technique that provides a more natural grasping method by letting the user manipulate a local proxy, such as a physical proxy prop linked to a neurological data set, so that moving the proxy moves the linked virtual object in the virtual world.
[5] World in miniature (WIM) is a type of indirect proxy that provides the user with a miniature handheld model of the virtual environment, which represents all objects in the virtual world, so manipulating an object in the miniature model manipulates the corresponding actual object in the virtual world.
[6] World in miniature (WIM) allows manipulation of virtual objects both within and outside the user's reach; for a distant object, the user does not need to select it, but can manipulate its representation in the miniature model, which then manipulates the distant object.
[7] Implementing world in miniature (WIM) for large and complex virtual environments is not very practical because creating the miniature model for such environments is very difficult.

[1] The third category of object selection techniques is image plane or volumetric selection.
[2] Image plane selection, also known as occlusion and framing, is a two-dimensional (2D) selection technique in which the user selects on a view plane that contains the object as viewed from a distance.
[3] In image plane selection, the user holds one or two hands or fingers between the eye and the desired object and provides a signal, such as a gesture or hand movement, to select the object when it lines up with the hand and the eye.
[4] The image plane selection techniques include the head crusher technique, the sticky finger technique, the lifting palm technique, and the framing hands technique, with framing hands being more common and the other techniques less common.
[5] In the head crusher technique, the user positions the thumb and forefinger so that they surround or enclose the desired object in the two-dimensional (2D) image plane.
[6] In the sticky finger technique, the object underneath the user's finger is selected.
[7] In the lifting palm technique, the user selects an object by flattening the outstretched hand and positioning the palm below the desired object as if trying to lift the object with the palm.
[8] In the framing hands technique, the user positions hands to form the two corners of a frame in the two-dimensional (2D) image surrounding an object, as typically seen while capturing movies or such visual media.
[9] Volumetric selection extends image plane selection by enabling the user to select a three-dimensional (3D) region in virtual space, with the objects within that region selected, where the region can be a box or cube, a sphere, or a cone.
[10] The cone casting flashlight technique is a volumetric selection technique that extends ray casting by casting a cone instead of a ray to a distance and selecting the objects within the cone.
[11] The cone casting flashlight technique can select multiple objects because the cone is volumetric, so selecting smaller or tightly grouped objects may be difficult.
[12] The sphere casting flashlight technique is a volumetric selection technique in which a sphere is cast onto the nearest intersected surface and the objects found within the sphere are selected.
[13] The two-handed box selection technique is a bimanual volumetric selection technique in which the user uses both hands to position, orient, and shape a box, usually a cube but possibly a rectangular parallelepiped, and progressively reduces it to select a specified region of three-dimensional (3D) space.
[14] Volumetric selection techniques are most useful for selecting small or well-defined isolated objects in a less complex virtual environment, and selecting smaller objects becomes problematic with any volumetric selection technique when the virtual environment is complex with many objects.

Facts:
[1] Integrated hybrid manipulation techniques are techniques that switch automatically from selection to manipulation after selection, without any explicit signal from the user, and switch back to selection mode after manipulation.
[2] Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER) is an integrated hybrid manipulation technique that mixes ray casting, a pointing-based selection method, with hand manipulation, so selection and manipulation are integrated and the user does not need to perform them separately.
[3] In Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER), the user selects an object using a ray casting technique, and when the ray intersects the desired object, the user's virtual hand moves automatically to the object and attaches to it, rather than the ray being attached to the object.
[4] In Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER), after the user's virtual hand attaches to the object, the technique switches to manipulation mode, allowing the user to change the object's position and orientation through hand manipulation.
[5] In Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER), manipulation ends when the user indicates to the system that the manipulation job is done through a trigger or a specific hand gesture, after which the virtual hand returns to its original position.
