Facts:
[1] Walking-based locomotion is a technique for traveling in a virtual environment in which physical walking or movement in the physical world is mapped to corresponding movement in the virtual environment.
[2] Walking-based locomotion is broadly divided into three categories: full gait techniques, partial gait techniques, and gait negation techniques.
[3] In full gait techniques, the user actually walks in the real world and that walk is translated to virtual movement in a virtual environment, which is the most natural way to travel.
[4] In full gait techniques, completely free walking is not practical or possible for virtual navigation, so walking is restricted within a specified limit in the physical space and translated to any amount of movement in a potentially infinite virtual space, creating a mismatch between physical and virtual movement.
[5] In a partial gait technique, the user walks in place, so the user does not change position and is not actually moving forward, backward, left, or right.
[6] Partial gait techniques require specialized devices in addition to other immersive hardware to provide input, may involve active walking interfaces such as pressure mats, pressure sensors, or interfaces with pressure sensors, and map the user's pattern of walking in a single place to different types of walking in the virtual space.
[7] Gait negation techniques require a specialized setup that cancels the user's lateral movements and keeps the user's physical position fixed, because natural walking involves lateral movement that may be difficult to map to a focused virtual movement, and the setup detects and eliminates the lateral movement before the movement is mapped to virtual navigation, making it easier for the system to understand the user's intention.
[8] Some examples of specialized setups used in gait negation techniques are a linear treadmill, motorized floor tiles, a human-sized hamster ball, and a friction-free platform.

[2] Selection-based locomotion has two types: target selection-based locomotion and route planning-based locomotion.
[3] In target selection-based locomotion, the user selects a destination or target, and the virtual viewpoint changes so that the user feels moved to the target.
[4] Target selection-based locomotion techniques include teleportation, which instantly changes the virtual viewpoint from the current location to the target location, map dragging, in which the user fixes a location to move there instantly, and the jumper technique in cave-type systems.
[5] Route planning-based locomotion is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the user selects a route to the target rather than only the endpoint; there may be multiple routes, and while moving through the selected route, different viewpoint changes make the user feel movement along a path, providing more granular control over travel and slightly more natural movement than target-based teleportation.
[6] Manipulation-based locomotion is a category of locomotion technique in which the user's position, orientation, or scale is manipulated using gestures that control either the virtual viewpoint or the virtual world.
[7] Manipulation-based locomotion can be implemented using a combination of the go-go technique, homer technique, and world in miniature metaphor.
[8] In a world in miniature metaphor, moving or manipulating certain objects causes a corresponding change in the virtual viewpoint, as if the user moves from one place to another.

Course: XR. Lecture System Design. Segment facts:
[1] In the island tour, each place is designed using a series of 360-degree images, so moving from one point to another is moving from one image to another.
[2] View interpolation ensures a smooth visual transition between two 360-degree images by blurring their boundaries, preventing the sudden movement or jerks that an unhandled image transition would cause and that reduce the user experience.
[3] Navigation arrows guide the user from one image to another, prevent random movement, and create a seamless exploration experience while supporting smooth travel.
[4] A virtual vehicle metaphor is a three-dimensional (3D) model of a vehicle that facilitates long-distance travel within the tour.
[5] Walking-based navigation is used for a single spot, but exploring the entire island by walking-based navigation would take a lot of time and may lead to cybersickness, so a different travel technique was required.
[6] The virtual vehicle travel technique gives the user a seated viewpoint inside the vehicle when it is selected, changes the surrounding scenes as the vehicle moves to create the feeling of motion, and lets the user operate the vehicle through ray casting interactions to provide a direction of movement and select a destination, to which the vehicle moves.
[7] The virtual vehicle travel technique is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the route is pre-planned and the user selects a destination to select a route; it is route selection, not target selection or instantaneous movement.

Facts:
[1] Prototypes can be broadly considered in two categories, horizontal prototypes and vertical prototypes.
[2] A horizontal prototype is a prototype that depicts the entire interface at a surface level, showing how the interface appears to the user in terms of look, feel, and appearance, without any functionality or interaction, so no real work can be done with it.
[3] Horizontal prototypes are suitable for discussing, brainstorming, and eliciting user feedback about the look, feel, and appearance of an interface, including whether its appearance is understandable, intuitive, and usable.
[4] A vertical prototype primarily represents interactions or functionalities by implementing a few selected features likely to be most commonly used in practice, in depth from the first screen to the last screen after the last action is performed, not all functionalities, because that would amount to having the full system.
[5] Vertical prototypes are suitable for analysis of interactions and features because they implement interactions.
[6] In the description of a vertical prototype, the term implemented and the term screen are generic, so implemented does not necessarily mean writing code, and screen can refer to a two-dimensional (2D) computer screen or a scene in a virtual or immersive environment.

Facts:
[1] A low-fidelity prototype is a prototype created without technological intervention, programming, code, or a computer, using non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood, and paper mockups of the look, feel, and functionality of an interface are a popular example.
[2] Low-fidelity prototyping provides a quick and cheap way to make and modify prototypes compared with approaches that require coding and computers, and it is used primarily to brainstorm alternative designs and obtain user feedback on usability.
[3] Low-fidelity prototyping is intuitively primarily associated with horizontal prototyping, but it is not limited to horizontal prototypes and can also be used to implement vertical prototypes.
[4] An interface sketch is a simple drawing that can be made on paper and depicts the major components of an interface, including the screen elements the user sees, buttons, selection options, their appearance, and their layout, so that an interface idea can be expressed to others or users for comments and feedback and its appearance can be envisioned.
[5] A single interface sketch is primarily used to represent a horizontal prototype and is not sufficient to prototype interactions because it does not show the sequence of user actions and the corresponding interface changes needed to execute a task.
[6] To represent interaction, a low-fidelity prototype needs a series of interface sketches rather than a single sketch, a practice often called storyboarding; a single sketch gives a horizontal prototype, whereas a series of sketches can give a vertical prototype depicting interaction.
[7] In a storyboard, each sketch is a keyframe, which is a snapshot of the interaction at a particular point in time; the keyframes visualize the interaction for a specific task and its corresponding scenes, and the storyboard captures the sequence of user actions and the screen appearances the user sees from the beginning of the task to its end.
[8] The overall purpose of a prototype is to convert an idea into a prototype, evaluate it, and revise the idea and prototype if evaluation finds issues; consequently, an interface sketch need not be replicated exactly in the final design, and feedback can change interface elements, their appearance, position, or layout.

[1] A medium-fidelity prototyping approach uses a computer to create simple prototypes without involving coding, whereas a low-fidelity prototyping approach does not rely on computers or digital media.

[4] In medium-fidelity prototyping, a computer used only to create static interface sketches produces a horizontal prototype because no real functionality is present, while an Adobe Flash animation video or a Microsoft PowerPoint (PPT) slideshow with simple key presses or timers can simulate interaction and create a vertical prototype.
[5] Low-fidelity prototypes are primarily meant for horizontal prototypes, medium-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for both horizontal and vertical prototypes, and high-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for vertical prototypes, so making horizontal prototypes using a high-fidelity approach may not make much sense.

[2] The prerequisites for performing quick or expert evaluation are at least a low-fidelity prototype, with higher-quality prototypes being better, and a team of evaluators.
[3] Quick evaluation is a usability test, but although the primary condition of usability testing is to involve users, the evaluation team for quick or expert evaluation is primarily the design team itself or skilled designers with knowledge and skill in the problem domain, and may optionally include a few end users.
[4] Quick or expert evaluation can rely on design-team members or domain experts rather than end users because they are assumed to have user-like experience, their feedback likely reflects users, and engaging them is less complicated, quicker, and cheaper than engaging a full evaluation team with end users.
[5] The evaluation team for expert evaluation should have at least three to five members; more members are welcome, but three to five is sufficient.
[6] In expert evaluation, each evaluator is presented with the prototype, evaluates it independently, and produces a report containing the usability issues perceived by that evaluator; the design team or team lead then combines these reports into a final list of usability issues.

Segment goal: Describe the After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) post-task questionnaire, its statements, rating scale, and averaging method.

Facts:
[1] The After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) is a post-task questionnaire consisting of three statements: 'I am satisfied with the ease of completing the tasks in this scenario'; 'I am satisfied with the amount of time it took to complete the tasks in this scenario'; and 'I am satisfied with the support information that is comprised of online help, messages, documentation when completing the tasks'.
[2] In the After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ), users rate each statement on a seven-point rating scale in which rating 1 means strongly disagree with the statement and rating 7 means strongly agree with the statement.
[3] The three statements of the After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) can be roughly mapped to the three usability measures in the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) definition: ease of completing the tasks relates to effectiveness, the amount of time taken to complete the tasks relates to efficiency, and the three statements together represent satisfaction.
[4] Feedback from the After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) can be summarised by taking either the average rating for each statement across all users who participated in the evaluation or the average rating for all statements taken together.

Facts:
[1] User evaluation is a quick evaluation technique that obtains feedback by asking users directly, and it requires user involvement, unlike expert evaluation techniques in which user involvement was optional.
[2] User evaluation is often called evaluation with self-reports, and user feedback is collected with rating scales, with the data sometimes called subjective or preference data.
[3] In user evaluation, collecting user feedback with rating scales is easy compared with more rigorous evaluation techniques.
[4] In user evaluation, the items provided to users to rate are questions or statements, and these items are commonly called questionnaires although they need not contain questions.
[5] One major concern in user evaluation is that identifying suitable questionnaires is challenging.
[6] In user evaluation, data can be collected after every task and at the end of the session, collecting data at both points is desirable if feasible, otherwise one of the two points must be chosen, and suitable questionnaires must be created for the point at which data are collected, so the questionnaires used after every task need not be the same as those used after the whole session.
[7] Well-known questionnaires available for post-task data collection include the After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ), designed by Lewis in 1991, and the Expectation Measure (EM), designed by Albert and Dixon in 2003.
[8] Well-known questionnaires available for post-session data collection include the System Usability Scale (SUS), designed by Brooke in 1996; the Computer System Usability Questionnaire (CSUQ), designed by Lewis in 1995; the Questionnaire for User Interface Satisfaction (QUIS), designed by Chin et al. in 1988; and the Usefulness Satisfaction and Ease of Use questionnaire (USE), proposed by Lund in 2001.

Facts:
[1] Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert evaluation technique and usability inspection method in which usability problems are identified by inspecting a prototype.
[2] A cognitive walkthrough requires at least a low-fidelity vertical prototype, a prototype that supports several tasks and may be low- or medium-fidelity, and an evaluation team of three to five members; a high-fidelity prototype is more welcome but involves more time and cost.
[3] A low-fidelity prototype for a cognitive walkthrough can be made as simple paper prototypes using the storyboarding approach, in which each prototype is a series of sketches depicting screen changes after each interaction, that is, a storyboard.
[4] In a cognitive walkthrough, a scenario or task description is created for the evaluators, and the task described in the scenario is converted into interface-level tasks, which are the actions that must be performed in the prototype to accomplish that task; the evaluators then perform those actions with the prototype.
[5] Usability questions are framed before a cognitive walkthrough to reflect usability issues, and evaluators use them as guidelines to identify problems users are likely to face while performing the tasks.
[6] For each usability question, evaluators must give a detailed report rather than a simple yes or no answer, explaining where they felt difficulty in the interface or interaction and why.
[7] The evaluators' reports are collected, combined, and analyzed at the end of the evaluation session to identify broader usability issues.

Facts:
[1] The System Usability Scale (SUS) is a post-session questionnaire, containing statements rather than questions, that is administered at the end of a session after users have completed all the tasks.
[2] The System Usability Scale (SUS) consists of 10 numbered statements: ... each even-numbered statement is the negatively worded counterpart of the preceding odd-numbered statement.
[3] Each System Usability Scale (SUS) statement is rated by the user on a 5-point agreement scale, where 1 indicates strongly disagree and 5 indicates strongly agree.
[4] The System Usability Scale (SUS) score S is calculated from all 10 statement ratings r_i, with i from 1 to 10, as S = 2.5 × (Σ...), where r_i is the user's rating for statement i.
[5] The System Usability Scale (SUS) score is interpreted directly as a percentage, and a score of 70% or higher is typically considered desirable, indicating that the interface is usable or has only minimal problems, while a score below 70% may indicate usability problems that may require a design review.
[6] Unlike expert evaluation techniques, which give designers more detailed reports from each evaluator, the System Usability Scale (SUS) gives a quick general indication from user ratings of whether usability problems exist but does not explain the reasons, so designers must identify the specific problems through further brainstorming or by examining the scores of individual statements.

[1] The Majuli VR Tour was developed with Unity engine version 2021.3.22f1 for the Oculus Quest 2 platform and Android smartphones, with Android 6.0 as the operating-system requirement for both versions.

[6] Because the Majuli VR Tour application was 5.1 gigabytes (GB) and not suitable for mobile deployment, a mobile version for Google Cardboard was made by compressing high-resolution 360-degree and two-dimensional (2D) images and removing most video playback support, reducing the application size to 0.7 gigabytes (GB).
[7] The Oculus Quest version of the Majuli VR Tour used 597 images, 11 cultural videos, 8 drone videos, and 5 360-degree videos, while the Google Cardboard mobile version used all 597 images in compressed form, no cultural videos, no drone videos, and 1 360-degree video for the initial experience.

We have course title Foundation for Virtual and Augmented Reality Systems. Lecture System Implementation. Segment goal describe user experience flow and features of three Majuli VR Tour demo implementations.

Facts:
[1] The Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour has three implementations: a 360-degree-image tour for the Oculus Quest headset, a three-dimensional (3D) model tour for the Oculus Quest headset, and a mobile-device tour using Google Cardboard.
[2] The 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation is for the Oculus Quest headset and uses 360-degree images, cultural videos, 360-degree videos, and ambient sound.
[3] In the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, the start screen uses a ray-casting-based selection method and plays introductory videos about Majuli and a tutorial that explains how to control and use the system.
[4] After user group selection in the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, the user experiences a boat ride from the mainland to Majuli island, using a 360-degree video captured during field trips.
[5] When the user reaches the riverbank in the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, a tablet interface appears that lets the user select a location on a map and move to that particular location.
[6] Inside a location in the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, the user can move forward and backward using arrow keys and can see icons intended to provide information.
[7] At different points in the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, cultural videos and activities are available, and a notification for cultural videos is played on the tablet interface.
[8] The 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation supports movement from one point to another using an overall island minimap on the tablet interface, in which each white dot represents a 360-degree image and the user's current location is marked in green.
[9] Travel from one point to another in the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation uses teleportation together with a vehicle-metaphor route-planning method, in which the road route is fixed and the user experiences motion as if riding a vehicle along the road.
[10] The three-dimensional (3D) model Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation is for the Oculus Quest headset and uses three-dimensional (3D) models to create the experience instead of 360-degree images and videos.
[11] The three-dimensional (3D) model Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation includes models of the entrance to Kamalabadi Satra, the entire campus with roads, and the villages and dwelling units.
[12] The three-dimensional (3D) models in the model-based Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation use textures from real images to create a realistic-looking appearance.
[13] The mobile-device Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation is for Google Cardboard, in which the user's smartphone is inserted into the Google Cardboard device to provide a 360-degree experience.
[14] The mobile-device Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation is a reduced form of the full Oculus Quest experience, with simpler controls and fewer features, but its navigation, selection, and manipulation modes are more or less the same.
[15] To optimize size in the mobile-device Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, most videos and cultural videos are omitted, and only some prominent videos are used.
[16] The mobile-device Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation retains the boat-ride experience and a tablet interface in a different form, with a minimap available at each place.

Facts:
[1] A testable research question, also called a hypothesis, is a question for which a study can be conducted to collect objective data, such as text entry speed, and draw objective conclusions independently of users' subjective interpretation.
[2] A non-testable research question, also called an untestable question, is a question that cannot be directly tested objectively because it depends on users' subjective interpretation and feedback, so a controlled experiment cannot be set up to collect objective data and, generally, a reliable scientific conclusion cannot be drawn.
[3] Research questions should not be framed from generalized concepts such as whether something is good, because such concepts are ambiguous and can lead to untestable questions.
[4] Testable research questions should be used instead of untestable questions, because user feedback on untestable questions is subjectively interpreted and generally cannot support a reliable, definite scientific conclusion, whereas testable questions allow reliable, definite conclusions.
[5] A more specific testable research question, such as whether one interface is faster than another, may answer a specific aspect but may not answer the broader generalized question of whether one interface is better, because faster and better are different concepts.
[6] To balance the trade-off between testability and generalization, stage 1 of an empirical study frames multiple testable research questions covering different aspects of a system and combines their conclusions to reach a definitive conclusion about a broader untestable generalized question, such as the overall goodness of an interface.

[4] A statistical significance test indicates whether an observed data difference is reliable by showing whether the difference is due to chance or to the tested conditions; a statistically significant difference is not due to chance, and a non-significant difference is due to chance.

[1] The method for performing a statistical significance test depends on the design of the experiment and the nature of the input data.
[2] The result of a statistical significance test can include the absolute difference in group means, the two-tailed p-value, the T value, the degrees of freedom, and whether the difference is statistically significant, and such results are typically reported, for example, as t = 1.70, p < 0.05, statistically significant, which is the standard way of representing any statistical significance test.
[3] In a statistical significance test, such as a paired sample t-test, the p-value is the probability of obtaining the data by chance, and a lower p-value means the result is less likely to have been obtained by chance.
[4] There are many statistical significance tests, which fall into two groups, parametric tests and non-parametric tests.
[5] For an experimental design with a nominal or categorical scale of measurement and one factor having two levels, the non-parametric chi-square test is used for a between-subject design, and the non-parametric McNemar's test is used for a within-subject design.
[6] For an experimental design with one factor having two levels and no other condition mentioned, a between-subject design can use the parametric independent samples t-test or the non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test, and a within-subject design can use the parametric paired sample t-test or the non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
[7] For between-subject designs, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used for one factor with more than two levels and factorial analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used for two or more factors each having two or more levels, and these two tests are parametric tests; the Kruskal-Wallis test can also be used for a between-subject design with one factor having more than two levels.
[8] For a within-subject design with one factor having three or more levels, or for a within-subject design with two or more factors each having two or more levels, the parametric repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) or the non-parametric Friedman test can be used.

[4] Optic flow is the speed at which the visual scene changes, and movement is perceived through this change in the view of the surroundings; in a virtual reality (VR) tour, user movement appears as a constantly changing scene.
[5] When the navigation in a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour is assumed to be walking, the scene-change speed (optic flow) should match the user's actual, or typical, real-world walking speed rather than VR walking speed; otherwise the movement looks unrealistic because it may be too fast or too slow.
[6] A more realistic system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour requires matching its optic flow to the user's instantaneous walking speed using a model of the user's typical walking behavior, because a constant optic flow is not very realistic as people rarely walk at constant speed.

[1] The virtual world part of a virtual experience is represented as a weighted graph G = (V, E), where V is the vertex set of all points of interest (POIs) and E is the set of weighted edges between POIs, representing a top view of the virtual world.
[2] The graph G used to represent the virtual world need not be complete, because in a realistic environment there may not always be a direct path from one place to another.
[3] For every pair of vertices v1 and v2 in the vertex set V, the assigned edge weight is the Euclidean distance between v1 and v2 if they are directly connected, and a very large number represented by the infinity symbol if they are not directly connected.
[4] In the mapping of the virtual world to the graph, each point of interest (POI) is a node, while a single object or structure is not necessarily a single node because it may contain multiple points of interest.
[5] The optimum travel path problem covering all points of interest (POIs) is to find a path P in the given graph G that covers all vertices in V, which are the POIs, and finishes in the least possible time while maintaining a realistic speed throughout, so that the user gets a realistic feeling.

Course: Foundation for VR and AR. Segment: VR experience optimisation. Goal: Describe factors that determine VR exposure duration and semi-interactive tour assumptions used to limit interaction time.
Facts:
[1] The duration of virtual reality (VR) exposure depends on the size of the virtual world, the travelling speed, the travelling time, and the interaction time spent inspecting, selecting, or manipulating virtual objects.
[2] A larger virtual reality (VR) environment leads to a longer duration of VR exposure because the user needs to cover a larger geographical area.
[3] Increasing the virtual travel or navigation speed reduces the duration of exposure to a virtual world because a higher speed lowers the time needed to travel and explore the entire geographical area.
[4] To provide a realistic walking experience in a virtual world, virtual travel speed cannot be modified arbitrarily; an arbitrary speed imposed on the user while navigating may not be a good idea.
[5] Teleportation-type movement in a virtual world can be the best choice for reducing overall exposure duration because it provides instantaneous movement between two points at maximum speed, but it is not a natural movement and may not always be a good approach when naturalness is required.
[6] Manipulating the virtual terrain or adjusting the distances between points of interest (POIs) can reduce travel time and therefore exposure time, but arbitrary terrain changes prevent users from perceiving the true size and feel of the real space and can hamper their mental map and wayfinding in the virtual world.
[7] In a purely system-automated or system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tool, users do not interact with virtual objects, so the interaction time required to interact with virtual objects can be ignored.
[8] A semi-interactive tour in virtual reality (VR) is a system-controlled navigation scenario in which travel is automatic, users may interact with objects after a navigation task is complete, and interaction is limited to a small set of objects at points of interest (POIs), while users cannot interact with other objects in the virtual environment.

[6] V naught is a constant for a given height h, equal to 2.1 h^2 divided by (0.157 * 1.72^2 * 1.8^2), where h is the user's height.

[1] For a path P in a graph that contains n vertices, the total travel time for P is the sum over i = 1 to n - 1 of the edge weight epsilon(v_i, v_{i+1}) between consecutive vertices, and epsilon(v_i, v_{i+1}) is the Euclidean distance between that pair of vertices.
[2] In the travel-time minimisation problem for a graph, the objective is to find a path P that contains all vertices of the graph with the minimum total travel time, and this problem is a variation of the travelling salesman problem (TSP).
[3] The travelling salesman problem (TSP) asks, given a complete graph, for the shortest possible path that visits each node exactly once and returns to the starting node, where the shortest path is defined by the total weight of the edges in the path.
[4] The graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem is not assumed to be a complete graph, so there may be no Hamiltonian path in that graph, where a Hamiltonian path is a path that covers all nodes and visits each node exactly once.
[5] For any two vertices in the graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem that are not directly connected, a hypothetical edge is introduced for computation, and the modified edge weight epsilon dash(v1, v2) is d(v1, v2), the Euclidean distance, if v1 and v2 are directly connected, or the shortest path length between v1 and v2 if they are not directly connected, where that shortest path length is the sum of the edge weights in the shortest path.
[6] The shortest path lengths used for the hypothetical edges are well-defined because the graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem is connected.

[2] The algorithm first converts the original graph G into a complete graph G' by keeping every directly connected edge unchanged and, for each pair of vertices that is not directly connected, adding a hypothetical edge whose length is the shortest path between those vertices in G.
[3] After the graph is complete, the algorithm replaces the Euclidean-distance edge weights with the travel time between each pair of vertices, producing a complete time-weighted graph G'' whose edge weights are travel times rather than Euclidean distances.
[4] The complete time-weighted graph G'' can be solved with a standard travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver, without needing a new algorithm, and the solver returns the optimal time tau_opt and the optimal path p_opt for that modified graph.

[6] The minimum travel time to cover all vertices, as computed by the algorithm that maps the original graph to a travelling salesman problem (TSP) instance, may still exceed the cybersickness time threshold when the terrain or virtual environment is large, so its purpose may be defeated in such cases.

Facts:
[1] There are two approaches to minimizing the possibility of cybersickness in a virtual world: finding a path that covers all points of interest in minimum time, and finding a path that covers the maximum possible points of interest within a given time limit.
[2] In the minimum-time approach, the virtual world is represented as a graph whose nodes are points of interest, whose directly connected edges are weighted by the Euclidean distance between the corresponding points of interest, and whose graph need not be complete.
[3] The problem of finding the minimum-duration travel that covers all points of interest in the virtual-world graph is mapped to the travelling salesman problem (TSP), a standard classical problem.
[4] In the minimum-time approach, travel times between pairs of vertices are computed using the natural walking speed model, so if the vertices are directly connected the model gives the travel time between them, and if they are not directly connected a hypothetical edge representing the shortest path between them is introduced and the travel time along that shortest path is computed using the model.
[5] In the minimum-time approach, the computed travel times become the weights of a complete graph formed by adding hypothetical edges, and this complete graph is given as input to a travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver, which outputs the optimum time and optimal path.
[6] The optimal path produced by the travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver may contain hypothetical edges, which must be removed before the final solution path is produced.
[7] The minimum-time approach that covers all points of interest may still produce a travel time beyond the threshold beyond which cybersickness may occur, motivating the use of a time limit in the alternative path optimization approach.

Course: Foundation for Virtual and Augmented Reality Systems. Segment about VR experience optimization, Majuli case study building graph from field-study data and applying TSP or VRPP solvers.

Facts:
[1] The Satra campus is modeled as a graph in which the points of interest (POI) are the nodes, the graph has at least 25 nodes, and the edges connecting pairs of nodes are weighted by the Euclidean distance between the corresponding points of interest.
[2] Converting the Satra site into a graph representation is an iterative process that requires detailed field study and revision of an initial graph.
[3] A team collected the Satra graph data through a field study, described as a kind of contextual inquiry, during the Kati Bihu festival, by observing people's travel and stopping behavior throughout the day, manually recording that behavior, and interviewing campus residents and Satra committee members about the places people typically visit and the places interviewees recommended to tourists.
[4] A point of interest (POI) in the Satra graph does not have to refer to an actual physical object; for example, a lake is not treated as a point of interest, but the corners of the lake are.
[5] When the first navigation optimization approach gives a minimum time above the time threshold, the second approach requires each point of interest (POI) node to be assigned a relative importance from discussions with people and an estimated maximum wait time from observed visitor behavior.
[6] The maximum wait time at a point of interest (POI) is the time a user needs to stop at the point of interest, inspect it, interact with it if possible, and resume navigation.
[7] Once the graph is obtained, a traveling salesman problem (TSP) solver can be used to find a minimum-time path covering all 25 nodes, or a vehicle routing problem with profits (VRPP) solver can be used to find a path within a chosen time threshold that covers the maximum number of most important points of interest while accounting for the maximum wait time at each point of interest.

Facts:
[1] The input to the optimal-path algorithm for a virtual environment is the original graph G, which is a fully connected graph but not necessarily a complete graph, with vertex set V, edge set E, and importance f and waiting time w specified for each node.
[2] The desired output of the algorithm is the optimal path P that maximizes the importance value F, covers the maximum number of most important points of interest (POIs), and keeps the total exposure time, i.e. the traveling time plus the waiting time, less than the time threshold.
[3] The first stage of the algorithm is to compute the complete graph G dash by replacing every pair of vertices that is not directly connected with the shortest path between those vertices.
[4] The algorithm then replaces the edge weights in the complete graph, which are originally the Euclidean distances between node pairs, with travel times t computed using the natural walking model, producing the final graph G double dash, whose edges are weighted by travel duration to give a realistic experience.
[5] The final graph G double dash, together with the importance f and waiting time w of each node, is given as input to a virtual reality path planning (VRPP) solver, and the solver returns the optimal path P_opt.
[6] The optimal path returned by the solver is modified by replacing each hypothetical edge between vertices V_i and V_j with the shortest path between those vertices in the original graph, and the algorithm returns this modified optimal path.

[2] In a generic graphics system, the host computer, or its central processing unit (CPU), has two-way communication with the display controller, in which the CPU sends display commands and may receive interaction data.
[3] The display controller is responsible for image generation, meaning it creates a representation of a scene as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed on a two-dimensional screen.
[4] Image generation is a multi-stage computational process, and if all rendering-related computations were carried out by the central processing unit (CPU), the CPU's time would be consumed by rendering, leaving it with very little time for other tasks and the system could do little except rendering; to avoid this and increase efficiency, rendering is usually carried out by a dedicated component.
[5] The dedicated rendering component is typically the graphics card, which usually contains its own graphics processing unit (GPU); in a generic graphics system this component is called the display controller, and the central processing unit (CPU) passes graphics rendering tasks to it so the computation takes place in the GPU rather than in the CPU.
[6] The display controller generates the image in a digital format, as strings of zeros and ones, and sends that image representation to video memory for storage.
[7] Video memory is the dedicated part of the overall memory hierarchy of the computer where the digital image is stored, typically as part of a separate graphics unit, and in modern graphics cards it is sometimes called video random-access memory (VRAM).
[8] A graphic display screen generally has a grid of picture elements, or pixels; when these pixels are activated, or excited, by an electrical or electromechanical means, they emit light with specific intensities that the viewer perceives as a colored image on the screen.
[9] The video controller uses the data stored in video memory to render an image on the screen, converting the digital image into some analog voltages required to activate the pixels, and it controls the pixel excitation mechanism using the video memory content.

[1] Graphic devices are broadly of two types, determined by the method used for excitation of pixels: vector scan devices and raster scan devices.
[2] Vector scan devices, also called random scan, stroke writing, or calligraphic devices, view an image as composed of continuous geometric primitives such as lines and curves and render the image by exciting only selected pixels that represent the primitives, on the assumption that rendering the primitives will make the whole image be perceived.
[3] Vector scan devices require high precision to target and excite specific pixels, which makes vector scan devices costly and typically unaffordable for mass production or mass consumption; vector scan devices are therefore typically used in specialized settings where limited quantities are required.
[4] A raster scan device views an image as represented by the whole pixel grid, activates all pixels in sequence, typically left to right and top to bottom, with appropriate inputs that make the pixels emit light at appropriate intensities, and the sequential activation of all pixels is called scanning or raster scanning.
[5] Raster scan rendering requires less precision and is much cheaper than vector scan rendering.
[6] Commercial products such as smartphones, televisions, and any device with a computer and display typically comprise raster scan displays.

Facts:
[1] The broad representation categories are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning-based representation.
[2] Point sample rendering is the simplest broad representation category, in which the captured scene information is represented as a set of raw data points on the scene, with each point carrying that information as attributes.
[3] In point sample rendering, the scene information is captured from the real world in the form of points using input sensors such as three-dimensional (3D) range scanners, range finders, or computer vision techniques.
[4] In point sample rendering, the captured points are processed or mapped to pixels to generate a synthetic image, relying on real-world information rather than synthetically defining objects.
[5] Boundary representation is a broad representation category in which objects are represented by the surfaces that define the object's boundary, and those surfaces can be polygonal or curved.
[6] Mesh representation is a popular boundary representation technique in which object surfaces are assumed to be polygons, the connected polygons form a mesh that represents the whole object, and a vertex or edge list stores all vertices or edges and their connections, allowing the object to be reconstructed.
[7] Objects with non-polygonal surfaces can be represented using mesh representation by approximating the surfaces with polygonal meshes, typically triangles, although other simple convex polygons may also be used.
[8] In mesh representation, a greater number of polygons gives a better approximation of the surfaces but makes the vertex list more complex and harder to construct, so a trade-off must be maintained.
[9] Mesh representation is the most basic form of representation for any object in a rendered scene used in computer graphics, and all other representations are converted to a mesh representation at the end of the pipeline before the objects are rendered.

Facts:
[1] A composite transformation matrix is used when constructing a world coordinate scene requires multiple basic geometric or modeling transformations, such as translation, rotation, scaling, or shearing.
[2] In the worked example, transforming rectangle ABCD from its local coordinate system to the chimney-like shape A′, B′, C′, D′ in the world coordinate scene cannot be done with one basic transformation and requires two basic transformations, scaling and translation.
[3] In the worked example involving rectangle ABCD and the transformed chimney shape A′, B′, C′, D′, the scaling matrix has Sx (the scaling factor along the x direction) equal to 0.5 and Sy (the scaling factor along the y direction) equal to 1 because the object is halved in length while its height remains unchanged, and the translation matrix has Tx (translation along the x-axis) equal to 5 and Ty (translation along the y-axis) equal to 5 because vertex D at (0, 0) moves to D′ at (5, 5).
[4] A composite transformation matrix is formed by arranging the individual transformation matrices from right to left according to the order of application: the first transformation applied is placed rightmost, each subsequent transformation is placed to its left, and the matrices are multiplied.
[5] In the worked example involving rectangle ABCD and A′, B′, C′, D′, scaling is applied first and translation is applied second, so the translation matrix is placed to the left of the scaling matrix and the two matrices are multiplied to obtain the composite transformation matrix.
[6] To obtain transformed vertices in the world coordinate scene, each current vertex is multiplied by the transformation matrix; in the worked example involving rectangle ABCD and A′, B′, C′, D′, A′ = M A, B′ = M B, C′ = M C, and D′ = M D, where M is the composite transformation matrix.
[7] Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so the right-to-left sequence of transformations must be set correctly; an incorrect sequence may produce an incorrect transformed result.

We have course: Foundation for VR/AR. Segment goal: Explain how ambient, diffuse, specular components are computed using reflection coefficients and vector dot products.
Facts:
[1] The intensity of light reflected from a surface and reaching the viewer's eye is a fraction of the incident light intensity, and this fraction is determined by the surface property known as the reflection coefficient or reflectivity.
[2] The simple lighting model defines three reflection coefficients: Ka for ambient light, Kd for diffuse reflection of direct light, and Ks for specular reflection of direct light.
[3] Each of the three reflection coefficients of the simple lighting model has a value from 0.0 to 1.0, where a value close to 0 represents a dull surface with no reflection because most of the light is absorbed, a value close to 1 represents a shiny, mirror-like surface where all light gets reflected, and varying the coefficients generates different effects between dull and shiny surfaces.
[4] The ambient component of the reflected light intensity is computed by multiplying the ambient light intensity falling on a surface point by the reflection coefficient for ambient light Ka.
[5] The diffuse reflection component is computed by multiplying the diffuse reflection coefficient for direct light Kd, the source light intensity Is, and the dot product of the surface normal vector N at the surface point from which light is reflected and the light source direction vector L, using that product only when N dot L is greater than 0 and otherwise setting it to 0, which means no diffuse reflection.
[6] The specular component is computed using an approximate model named after its inventor, Phong.
[7] The angle phi in the specular calculation is the angle between the viewer direction vector V and the ideal specular reflection direction vector r, which is the direction a mirror would reflect the light, and cos phi is the dot product V dot r.
[8] The specular component is computed as the specular reflection coefficient for direct light Ks times the source light intensity Is times the dot product of the viewer direction vector V and the ideal specular reflection direction vector r, raised to the power Ns, and it is 0 when V dot r is not greater than 0.
[9] The ideal specular reflection direction vector r is represented by r equal to twice the dot product of the light source direction vector L and the surface normal vector N, multiplied by the surface normal vector N, minus the light source direction vector L.

[1] In lighting, the intensity of light from a source typically diminishes with the distance from the source to a surface point, so an intensity attenuation factor over distance is needed.
[2] The radial intensity attenuation factor accounts for the diminishing of light intensity with distance and is typically computed as an inverse quadratic function of the distance d between the light source and the surface point, using coefficients a0, a1, and a2 that can be varied for a more realistic effect.
[3] Angular intensity attenuation is considered primarily for generating spotlight effects, in which elements inside the spotlight region are visible or brightly visible and elements outside the spotlight zone are darker.
[4] A commonly used angular intensity attenuation factor is 0 when the surface point is outside the angular limit theta, the range of the spotlight cone, and when the surface point is within that angular limit it varies as the cosine of phi raised to the power A1, where A1 is a positive angular attenuation exponent that can be varied to achieve different effects.
[5] In the simple lighting model modified for radial and angular intensity attenuation, the I_M intensity component is left unchanged, while the sum of the diffuse reflection component I_D and the specular reflection component I_SPEC is multiplied by the radial and angular attenuation factors; if those factors are 1, the model reduces to I_M + I_D + I_SPEC.

[3] The basic idea of view transformation, which is the viewing pipeline, is that an image on a screen or head-mounted display (HMD) is produced by selecting a portion of a three-dimensional (3D) scene and projecting the portion onto a two-dimensional (2D) display or view plane.
[4] The viewing pipeline consists of a viewing transformation that defines a view coordinate system and transforms a scene from a three-dimensional (3D) world coordinate system to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, a projection transformation that projects the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate scene to a two-dimensional (2D) view plane or two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, a window-to-viewport transformation that maps the projected scene to a two-dimensional (2D) device coordinate space, and the operations clipping and hidden surface removal, which in the described pipeline take place in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system.
[5] The sequence of stages or sub-stages in the viewing pipeline is not fixed, because different implementations can alter the sequence.

We have course VR resource optimization, segment about window-to-viewport transformation.

Facts:
[1] A window is the same as a normalized clipping window, is another term for the view plane, and is an abstract intermediate representation that has nothing to do with the display.
[2] A viewport is not defined on the view plane but in device space as a portion of the final screen where the scene will be rendered, and it is defined with respect to the screen or display origin and the screen or display dimensions.
[3] The window-to-viewport transformation maps a point from the abstract window representation to a device-specific viewport representation, specifically from a window point (Wx, Wy) to a viewport point (Vx, Vy).
[4] In the window-to-viewport transformation, the transformation matrix is a three by three matrix whose Sx is defined in terms of the viewport and window dimensions along the x-axis, whose Sy is similarly defined with respect to the viewport and window dimensions along the y-axis, and whose Tx and Ty are computed in terms of Sx and Sy and the corresponding x-axis or y-axis window and viewport dimensions.
[5] To obtain the transformed viewport point, the window point vector is multiplied by the window-to-viewport transformation matrix, and because the resulting point is in homogeneous coordinate representation, the Cartesian point is obtained by dividing the result by the homogeneous factor W.

[1] In point rendering, a point represented by real-number coordinates is mapped to the nearest integer coordinate values, which maps from device space to discrete space; this rounding method is suitable for points but not for other geometric shapes such as lines and circles.
[2] A naive line-rendering method requires many floating-point operations, and because floating-point operations slow down a computer, the objective of efficient line-rendering algorithms is to avoid floating-point operations.
[3] Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm is a popular line-rendering algorithm that identifies the pixels that approximately represent a line without using floating-point operations.
[4] The Bresenham line-drawing algorithm is described for line slopes between -1 and +1, with minor modification needed for other slopes; its input is the two line endpoints and its output is the set of pixels that approximate the line segment.
[5] In Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm for line slopes between -1 and +1, the algorithm first computes delta x, the difference between the two endpoints' x coordinates, delta y, the difference between their y coordinates, and the decision parameter p, defined as twice delta y minus delta x; it initializes x and y to the first endpoint's x and y coordinates and adds that pixel to the output pixel set; then, in a loop until the other endpoint is reached, if p is less than 0 it increments x by 1 and resets p to the older p plus twice delta y, otherwise increments x and y by 1 and resets p to the older p plus twice delta y minus twice delta x, adding each computed coordinate to the output pixel set.
[6] Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm is efficient and speeds up line rendering because it uses integer arithmetic, such as addition and multiplication, and avoids floating-point operations such as rounding, division, and sometimes floating-point multiplication.
[7] Speeding up line rendering makes the system more efficient because at any instant a system may need to render a large number of line segments, and in interactive graphics such as virtual reality each user input can change the scene and require redrawing hundreds of thousands of lines.
[8] Similar efficient rendering algorithms exist for other geometric shapes, such as circles, ellipses, filled areas, and polygons, and they are more complex than line rendering.
[9] The basic idea for rendering a shape on a screen is to map the original shape to the set of pixels that represent it as fast as possible by reducing floating-point operations.
[10] For lines, floating-point operations can be completely eliminated, whereas for other shapes they may not be completely eliminated but can be minimized.

We need list concepts in facts. Course: Foundation VR/AR. Segment goal: GPUs exploit parallelism to execute transformation, lighting, projection, rasterization, texturing, hidden-surface removal efficiently.
Facts:
[1] A graphics processing unit (GPU) is the processing unit of a separate graphics card, with its own memory elements, that is used in computer graphics and virtual reality to exploit the inherent parallelism of graphics operations, which are highly parallel, whereas central processing units (CPUs) are generally not designed for large-scale parallel activities, although modern CPUs have some parallel features.
[2] A GPU is typically a multicore system in which many cores, each capable only of simple integer and floating-point arithmetic, work simultaneously on one single instruction and produce data simultaneously, and groups of cores form streaming multiprocessor units, each containing several cores.
[3] A GPU is broadly organized with a host, input assemblers and a thread execution manager, where the manager allocates work to many streaming multiprocessors, each of which has a parallel data cache, and a texture storage stores predefined surface colors, with the elements exchanging data with global memory through load and store information.
[4] The GPU performs modeling transformation by applying transformations such as rotation, multiplying the same transformation matrix with each vertex vector simultaneously for all vertices, producing a stream of transformed triangles from local coordinates to world coordinates, which gives a significant performance gain in real-time rendering because millions of vertices need to be processed per second and even more for a realistic immersive experience.
[5] Most graphics systems assume that a scene to be rendered is made of triangles, so surfaces are converted into triangular meshes regardless of how a developer defines an object, and the GPU assumes such a mesh as input.
[6] Graphics libraries provide application programming interfaces (APIs) through which triangles in a mesh are sent to the GPU one vertex at a time, and the GPU assembles the vertices into triangles.
[7] The GPU computes vertex color by performing vector dot products, as in the simple lighting model, simultaneously for multiple vertices.
[8] The GPU projection stage combines viewing transformation, projection transformation and viewport transformation in a composite matrix multiplied with vertices, producing a stream of triangles in screen or device coordinates, a continuous coordinate space, ready to be converted to pixels.
[9] In rasterization, the pixels overlapped by device-space triangles are determined, and algorithms exploit the fact that each pixel can be treated independently from all other pixels so that the colors of all pixels can be determined simultaneously in parallel.
[10] In the GPU pixel processing stage, the two activities that take place are surface texturing and hidden surface removal.
[11] In the pixel processing stage, the simplest surface texturing method applies stored texture images to the geometry being rendered by replacing the computed pixel color with the texture color at the corresponding texture point; GPUs store textures in high-speed texture storage on the graphics card, which each pixel calculation must access, and because nearby pixels tend to access nearby texture image locations, specialized memory caches reduce access time.
[12] In the pixel processing stage, hidden surface removal uses a depth buffer algorithm in which a dedicated depth buffer stores the depth information for points in a three-dimensional (3D) scene before projection onto a two-dimensional (2D) plane, where depth is the viewer's distance with respect to each pixel.

We have course: Foundation for Virtual and Augmented Reality Systems. Segment goal: Describe how Unity's built-in render pipeline supports object definition through model files, meshes, materials, and textures.
Facts:
[1] Unity's built-in render pipeline supports object definition by providing models, which are files containing data on the shape and appearance of three-dimensional (3D) objects and are essentially the object representation.
[2] A Unity model file can contain mesh, material, and texture data, and, if the object represents an animated character, it can also contain animation-related data.
[3] Unity supports more than 10 standard and proprietary model file formats, including the .fbx format, the .dae format, the .dxf format, and the .obj format, so models created in different formats can be imported into Unity and made to work.
[4] In Unity, three-dimensional (3D) meshes are the main graphics primitives, and Unity supports triangulated or quadrangulated polygonal meshes, meaning meshes whose polygons are triangles or quadrangles.
[5] In Unity's mesh rendering workflow, the mesh renderer takes geometry from the mesh filter and renders it at the position defined by the game object's transform component.
[6] In a Unity model file, materials describe the appearance of an object's surface by specifying how the surface should be rendered, including references to textures used, tiling information, color tints, and other information, whereas meshes describe the object's shape.
[7] In Unity, textures are bitmap images applied over a mesh surface as a way to assign colors to the surface, and they can represent many other aspects of a material's surface in addition to basic color, such as reflectivity and roughness.

[4] A skybox in Unity is a sky background that a camera draws before it renders a frame; it is a cube with different textures on its faces to create the feel of a 360-degree environment, and Unity always renders the skybox at the back.
[5] Unity provides support for realistic lighting on game objects, allowing developers to specify the intensity, direction, and color of the light and to render real-time shadows using shadow mapping.
[6] In the Unity developer environment, visual effects can be applied to the camera, game objects, light sources, and other elements of the game.
[7] The halo effect is a visual effect that creates light areas around light sources, typically to give the impression of small dust particles in the air.
[8] The lens flare effect is a visual effect that simulates the effect of lights refracting inside a camera lens.
[9] The line renderer effect is a visual effect that takes an array of two or more points in 3D space and draws a straight line between those points, enabling anything from a simple straight line to a complex spiral to be drawn.
[10] View transformation, also called the viewing pipeline, is an important stage in the 3D graphics pipeline.
[11] Unity supports view transformation through its camera concept; after a developer sets up a camera, Unity performs the other calculations automatically.
[12] In Unity, a camera is created by adding a camera component to a game object.

Course: Foundation for VR/AR. Segment goal: Explain why Unity scripting support needed for customized XR experiences and how to set up C# scripting environment to create and attach scripts.
Facts:
[1] In the Unity development environment, built-in support gives a good-quality experience that is only what the system provides, so to obtain a more customized experience according to the programmer's expectations and needs, the programmer must write scripts or small pieces of code to change the built-in support.
[2] Unity's scripting environment is set up automatically when the Unity package is installed, Unity supports integrated development environments (IDEs) such as Visual Studio, Visual Studio Code, and JetBrains Rider, and on Windows and Mac the default Unity installation also installs Visual Studio, which can be used to develop and compile scripts.
[3] The scripting language supported by Unity is C#, which is an object-oriented programming language created by Microsoft.
[4] In Unity, a C# script can be attached as a component to a game object to control the behavior or activities of that object, and creating a C# script is essentially creating a new type of component that can be attached to game objects, providing a component that behaves as desired rather than according to the built-in support provided by the environment.
[5] Once a C# script is attached as a component to a game object in Unity as part of the design or development, it starts working whenever the game is executed, and it allows the developer to trigger game events, modify component properties over time, and respond to user input in any way the developer wants.
[6] Unlike most other assets, C# scripts in Unity are usually created directly within Unity, using the interface provided by the integrated development environment (IDE), by choosing Assets, then Create, then C# Script from the main menu, and the new script is created in the folder selected in the project panel when the project is started.

Course: Foundation for VR/AR Systems. Segment goal: basic structure of a Unity C# script and inspect variable values and console output.
Facts:
[1] A Unity C-sharp (C#) script file begins with a namespace component, with using statements such as using Unity engine and using system.collections, and defines a public class, typically inherited from MonoBehaviour, whose name is the same as the file name.
[2] A Unity script contains a Start function that is called whenever the script is called, as the starting point, and an Update function that is called in each frame and is invoked whenever the script executes and some change happens.
[3] In a Unity script, the Vector3 data type represents the position of a three-dimensional (3D) point by storing three coordinates as three elements of a vector.
[4] In Unity, a developer can see the code in a script file by double-clicking the script asset and can check variable values in the Inspector interface on the Unity Hub editor.
[5] In a Unity script, the Debug.Log function prints a message to the console output, which can be seen after running the game or application or after the script has been executed.

[8] Superimposition-based markerless augmented reality (AR) applications recognize one or multiple physical objects using computer vision techniques and superimpose digital content on the real-world scene depending on the recognized objects.
[9] Projection-based markerless augmented reality (AR) applications use light projectors to project digital graphics, digital characters, or other digital content onto an object, a surface, or a space, such as in holographic projection.
[10] Outlining-based markerless augmented reality (AR) applications use object recognition to recreate the user's immediate surroundings and digitally enhance the view, for example by showing cars around a driver that are not clearly visible in low-light conditions.

[1] In virtual reality (VR), an external factor in cybersickness (CS) is a factor that is not subjective to a user's mental or physical condition, and hardware is one category of external factors.
[2] Cybersickness (CS) in virtual reality (VR) is not simply a problem of inferior hardware quality; although early users associated it with inferior hardware, many problems persist with advanced technology, so some aspects of devices themselves induce cybersickness.
[3] Display resolution is a hardware factor that reduces cybersickness (CS) up to a certain point; a study evaluating 1K, 2K, 3K, and 4K resolutions found a substantial reduction in CS induction from 1K to 2K, but no significant further reduction from 2K to 3K or from 3K to 4K.

[1] Measurement techniques for cybersickness (CS) rely on three components: the input provided for measurement, the measurement technique itself, and the output generated.
[2] Inputs for measuring cybersickness (CS) can be questionnaire-based, physiological and biometric information, behavioral information, and content-based information.
[3] The measurement technique or evaluation process for cybersickness (CS) can be manual, automated, machine learning-based, or real-time evaluation while the experience is taking place.
[4] The output of cybersickness (CS) measurement can be binary classes, multiple classes, or a sickness score that is a number.
[5] Questionnaire-based input for measuring cybersickness (CS) is a common method that uses self-report questionnaires or scales, generally in the form of ratings, to rate users' discomfort or disorientation on a numerical scale.
[6] Questionnaire-based cybersickness (CS) scales are easy to administer and help researchers or practitioners better understand the causes of cybersickness and identify potential interventions.
[7] Questionnaire-based cybersickness (CS) scales are typically administered before or after an experience, can also be administered during the experience, with before and after being the most common timing and during being occasional.
[8] The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) is one of the most extensively used questionnaires for measuring cybersickness (CS).
[9] The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) contains 16 items divided into three subscales: the oculomotor subscale, the disorientation subscale, and the nausea subscale.
[10] In the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ), participants rate the intensity of individual symptoms belonging to the oculomotor, disorientation, and nausea subscales on a scale from 0 to 3, where a higher score denotes more severe symptoms.
[11] The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) was not originally designed for virtual reality (VR) but was adapted for use in the context of virtual reality.
[12] Questionnaires specifically designed for virtual reality (VR) include the Virtual Reality Sickness Questionnaire (VRSQ) and the Cyber Sickness Questionnaire (CSQ), which is good for evaluating virtual reality experiences with head-mounted displays (HMDs).
[13] Shorter and more concise questionnaires used to assess specific conditions include the Misery Scale (MIS) and the Fast Motion Sickness Scale (FMS).
[14] Questionnaires used to measure susceptibility to cybersickness (CS) include the Motion History Questionnaire (MHQ), the Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (MS-SQ), and the Visually Induced Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (VIMS or VIMS-SQ).
[15] Questionnaires commonly used to assess overall discomfort include the Nausea Scale and the Motion Sickness Assessment Questionnaire (MSAQ).

[1] Cybersickness (CS) is subjective and individual susceptibility to cybersickness varies, so a one-size-fits-all approach or developer-side interventions alone may not be sufficient and users need their own countermeasures to reduce the effects of cybersickness.
[2] To reduce the risk of cybersickness (CS), users may be advised to avoid continuous or long-duration exposure to a virtual environment, and studies suggest that the generally safe maximum duration of a virtual reality (VR) session for the majority of users likely to suffer from cybersickness is between 55 and 70 minutes, although the exact duration may vary with device, content, and other factors, and longer exposure is risky.
[3] Habituation is the gradual decrease in the intensity of cybersickness (CS) after repeated experience in a virtual environment.

[16] Phantom legs is a hardware-level alteration that applies alternating haptic cues synchronized to users' footsteps using additional hardware, and it was found to reduce cybersickness (CS) to a great extent.
[17] Floor vibrations are a hardware-level alteration for reducing cybersickness (CS) that uses vibration-driven whole-body tactile feedback to match the vibrations of the virtual environment.
[18] Simultaneous presentation of sound and vibration is a hardware-level alteration that has been tried for reducing cybersickness (CS), for example in a walking vibe system that uses two small vibration motors behind the ears for vibrotactile feedback during a walking experience.
[19] Modified motion platforms are a hardware-level alteration in which short bursts of rotational acceleration matching visual forward acceleration were found quite effective in reducing cybersickness (CS), and the platforms can be modified to produce this effect.
[20] Locomotion techniques can play a crucial role in preventing cybersickness (CS), and they can be modified or new techniques can be proposed to reduce its effect.

[1] Non-hand input techniques in virtual reality (VR) consist of head tracking, eye tracking, full-body tracking, and sound-based tracking.
[2] Full-body tracking is a non-hand input method in virtual reality (VR) that tracks full-body movement, more than the head, hands, and eyes.
[3] Full-body tracking can add to the illusion of self-embodiment and social presence in a virtual world because its output can show the user a fuller representation of themselves.
[4] There are two broad approaches to full-body tracking: a motion capture suit (MOCAP) and camera-based tracking.
[5] In a motion capture suit (MOCAP) approach to full-body tracking, sensors in the suit capture and transmit raw movement data, which are combined and converted into full-body position and movement; for example, the Perception Neuron suit uses straps with inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors on the legs, hands, arms, and head.
[6] In camera-based full-body tracking, multiple surrounding cameras observe an actor wearing a suit with fiducial markers, typically reflective markers, and infer the actor's overall body movement from the markers' movement; OptiTrack and Microsoft Kinect are examples of such camera-based full-body tracking systems.
[7] Sound-based tracking is a non-hand input technique in virtual reality (VR) that captures voice, speech, and non-speech sound for interaction using simple microphones or microphone arrays, which are sets of microphones that capture sound in a 360-degree environment.

We have facts:
[1] Audio output is an output device typically used in a virtual reality (VR) setup, and it can provide specialized three-dimensional (3D) audio for a sense of where sounds are coming from, with speakers fixed in space or moving with the head, and headphones are preferred for a fully immersive system because the sound source can change with head movement.

[2] Haptic rendering systems are outputs that activate touch sensation and explore touch perception, and haptic outputs can be categorized as passive versus active, tactile versus proprioceptive, and self-grounded versus world-grounded devices.

[3] Passive haptic devices are static real-world physical objects that match the shape of virtual objects and are not controlled by the computer, whereas active haptic devices are physical objects or physical feedback controlled by the computer that provide a sense of touch when interacting with virtual objects.

[4] Tactile haptics are haptic devices that provide touch sensations through the skin, and they include vibrotactile stimulation, which uses mechanical vibration of the skin, and electrotactile stimulation, which uses electrodes that pass current through the skin.

[4] The three broad types of visual displays are head-mounted displays (HMDs), which are wearable and mobile, world-fixed displays, which are not wearable and are stationary, and regular displays, which are mobile or can be stationary.
[5] Although head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be used as input to track head motion, their primary use is as a display device.
[6] A head-mounted display (HMD) is a sophisticated piece of equipment that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components within its package.
[7] A head-mounted display (HMD) places images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens, with one screen providing monoscopic viewing and two screens providing stereoscopic viewing, and stereoscopic HMDs are more common than monoscopic HMDs.
[8] Head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be further categorized into three types: non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through.
[9] Non-see-through HMDs are typically used in virtual reality (VR), optical see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented reality (AR), and video see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented virtuality, in which real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment.
[10] A world-fixed display renders graphics onto a surface or screen that is fixed and does not move with the user's head; the display is not moving, while the user can move within a physical space.
[11] World-fixed displays range from standard monitors to displays that completely surround the user, typically called a cave.
[12] The fish tank display, developed in 1993, is an early world-fixed virtual reality (VR) display that uses a fixed cathode-ray tube (CRT) monitor as the output and an optical head tracker and a haptic device as inputs, so that the stereo perspective view of a 3D scene changes as the user's head moves.
[13] A more recent world-fixed display example is the surround screen, or cave system, which typically has three to six large screens around the user for visual immersion and is usually driven by a single or group of powerful graphics engines and requires elaborate tracking of the user's movements.
[14] Regular displays, which can be mobile or stationary, refer to common tablets or smartphones, are not specialized, are typically relevant for non-immersive virtual reality (VR), and are mostly used for augmented reality (AR).

[2] In the calibration stage for inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors, the objective is to make the measured angular velocity (omega_g) and the actual angular velocity (omega_a) as close as possible, which means reducing the measurement error to as small a value as possible.

[3] One simple calibration model assumes a linear relationship between measured angular velocity (omega_g) and actual angular velocity (omega_a), for example omega_g = a + b omega_a, where the ideal condition omega_g = omega_a corresponds to a = 0 and b = 1, but this ideal condition never happens in practice and the linear relationship is not the only possible relationship.

[4] The presented calibration uses many, sometimes thousands, paired samples from two sensors: a cheap, inaccurate inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor that produces the measured values (omega_g), and an expensive, highly accurate benchmark sensor that produces the actual values (omega_a), although the benchmark is very close rather than exact or ideal.

[5] A simple calibration method compares the paired samples by computing, for n pairs, the sum of the squared differences between the expression C1 + C2 omega_g and the actual values omega_a, and it finds the constants C1 and C2 that minimize this sum; this classical optimization is linear least squares regression, one of many techniques that is used here for simplicity.

[6] After the constants C1 and C2 are determined, calibration mathematically transforms the cheap sensor reading into a calibrated value omega_cal, defined as omega_cal = C1 + C2 omega_g, mapping the inexpensive measured angular velocity omega_g to the closest possible match with the actual value rather than by using an actually expensive or highly accurate sensor.

[1] Registration is the step that finds the initial pose or initial orientation of the sensor or user and sets the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds, represented as theta at t = 0.
[2] A simplifying assumption for understanding registration is that the direction the headset is facing when the tracking system is turned on is taken as the initial orientation, with the initial alignment set to the forward direction.
[3] Registration can be aided by fiducial markers, reflectors, or tags; it can also be performed without them using computer vision techniques, and the process is simpler when such aids are present.
[4] Integration is the stage that computes the current sensor orientation theta_t at time t = k delta_t by adding to the initial orientation estimated during registration, theta_0, the sum of calibrated angular velocity samples W_cal_i times the sampling interval delta_t over the elapsed samples; the sensor data stream usually arrives at regular discrete intervals, and k is an integer.
[5] A calibrated angular velocity sample W_cal_i is the angular velocity sample from a gyroscopic sensor at instant i, and it indicates a change in orientation equal to W_cal_i multiplied by the sampling interval delta_t.
