[1] Virtual reality (VR) input devices are broadly divided into hand input devices, which require hands to operate, and non-hand input devices, which do not require hands to operate.
[2] Hand input devices in virtual reality (VR) fall into five broad categories: world-grounded devices, non-tracked handheld controllers, tracked handheld controllers, hand-worn devices, and bare-hand inputs.
[3] World-grounded hand input devices are devices that are fixed in the real world and do not move; a joystick is an example that is commonly used to interact with desktop or other grounded systems, and portability is an issue because they constrain the user to move within a specified area.
[4] Non-tracked handheld controllers are hand input devices that are held in the hand but are not tracked in three-dimensional (3D) space, so the system does not know their exact position with respect to a reference frame; examples include buttons, joysticks, triggers, and traditional video game controllers.
[5] Non-tracked handheld controllers can cause break-in presence because the user's untracked hand movements may not produce a corresponding change in the position of the virtual hands in the virtual world, creating discomfort about whether the user is performing the task appropriately and affecting the perception of presence in the virtual world.
[6] Tracked handheld controllers are hand input devices with six degrees of freedom tracking, so the system can track their movements; input controllers that come with modern virtual reality (VR) systems are tracked devices so that break-in presence is avoided, and VIVE controllers are an example because they combine a joystick with tracking and are mainly used in VR.
[7] Tracked handheld controllers have the limitation that users cannot directly or fully touch and feel passive virtual objects through tangible interaction because the user's hands are occupied with the controller, although force feedback controllers may sometimes resolve the issue.
[8] Hand-worn hand input devices are devices that are worn on the hands, arms, or fingers; examples include data gloves, electromyography (EMG) bands, and rings, with data gloves being more popular.
[9] Bend-sensing data gloves are data gloves with sensors at all bend positions or joints and other positions; their processing unit receives continuous raw data from these bend sensors and processes it to detect hand postures and gestures, and because their many sensors make any gesture likely to generate a different data stream for unambiguous interpretation, they provide a large degree of freedom that can make interaction more natural than controller-based interaction.
[10] Pinch gloves are data gloves in which the sensors are placed only at fingertip positions, which may vary but often include the thumb and index finger fingertips; they detect a limited set of pinch gestures, are good at determining whether the fingertips are touching, and are typically used for discrete input such as object selection and mode switching.
[11] The advantages of hand-worn hand input devices are natural input with potentially rich gesture interaction, comfortable hand positions, no line-of-sight issue unlike some controller-based input, and the ability of the user's hands and fingers to fully interact with real objects, making different sorts of perception possible.
[12] Issues with hand-worn hand input devices are that recognizing many gestures requires users to recalibrate often or to learn and remember many gestures, which can create problems for different user categories, and that long exposure time can become uncomfortable because the hands may become sweaty.
[13] Bare-hand inputs are the most natural hand input interactions: the system tracks the user's bare hand using computer vision techniques, the user does not need to wear anything or use any external device, and computer vision algorithms detect the user's gestures and translate them into commands in the virtual environment, leaving the user's hands completely free.
[14] The Leap Motion device is an example of a bare-hand input device: it is an infrared (IR)-based hand-tracking sensor that typically contains three IR light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and two wide-angle cameras; the LEDs generate IR light reflected from the hands and picked up by the cameras, and software converts the signals into gestures.
[15] The Leap Motion device can be attached to a head-mounted display (HMD) to provide hand input support even if the HMD does not support hand input, and it is typically useful with low-cost HMDs that do not provide good-quality controllers or controller support, such as cardboard-type devices in which a smartphone provides a stereoscopic view and which do not support interaction.
[16] The Leap Motion device has problems: fatigue may occur from holding hands in front of its sensor or camera, the hand must be in the line of sight of its camera, and consistent recognition of gestures across a wide range of users may be an issue.

Course: VR Software segment. Facts:
[1] To build a virtual reality (VR) experience, a developer can either build a virtual world generator (VWG) from scratch using a basic software development kit (SDK) for a specific headset, device, or platform, or use a ready-made virtual world generator (VWG) customized by choosing menu options and writing high-level scripts.
[2] A basic software development kit (SDK) for a headset, device, or platform is typically expected to provide basic drivers to drive the hardware, interfaces or application programming interfaces (APIs) to access tracking data, and application programming interfaces (APIs) to make calls to graphical rendering libraries; in a virtual world generator (VWG), basic drivers and tracking cover some aspects and rendering covers other aspects, but not every aspect of locomotion or matched motion, physics, or networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience is typically taken care of by the software development kit (SDK).
[3] When building a virtual world generator (VWG) from a basic software development kit (SDK), the developer must build, at the very least, the physics support of the virtual world from scratch, handling problems such as movement of an avatar, collision detection, occurrence of collision and the response to it, lighting models, and audio support; sometimes collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience support is also required.

[1] Plugins to existing tools are a category of augmented reality (AR) software in which a plugin is added to an existing interactive two-dimensional (2D) or three-dimensional (3D) content authoring tool that may not itself support AR content or system development, and the plugin adds AR-specific functions such as tracking, visualization, and 3D registration of digital content over the real-world view, while relying on the main authoring tool for content authoring.
[2] Plugins to existing tools provide an easy and quick method for developing augmented reality (AR) applications when the developer already knows the host authoring tool, because the developer can rely on knowledge of the original tool and only needs to understand the plugin, reducing the required understanding of the system; if the developer does not know the authoring tool, the approach makes no sense because everything must be learned from scratch.
[3] Many interactive three-dimensional (3D) graphics authoring tools, including Unity, Vizard, and Lumion, are used to create interactive 3D applications, and most of these tools have plugins for augmented reality (AR) visualization; Unity has the widest range of available solutions for AR visualization.
[4] The augmented reality (AR) Toolkit for Unity from the AR Tool Works is an example of an AR plugin for Unity that provides marker-based tracking, image-based or computer-vision-based tracking, and AR visualization support.
[5] Vuforia is a tracking library that has an augmented reality (AR) plugin that works with Unity three-dimensional (3D) and can be used to create AR applications, particularly mobile AR applications for iOS and Android platforms.
[6] Limitations of using plugins to add augmented reality (AR) support to existing content authoring tools are that user interface and interaction design can be limited to what the underlying authoring tool provides, software and hardware configuration depends on that tool, and content produced with the authoring tool usually becomes dependent on proprietary player software in most cases.
[7] A way to resolve the limitations of higher-level augmented reality (AR) tools or plugins is to use low-level software development tools, such as software libraries, and build the system from scratch rather than depending on a third-party tool, an approach that applies to any higher-level tool.

[1] The human eye contains a cornea that acts as a powerful lens with fixed focal depth, a natural lens with variable focal depth, and a non-planar retina that is the image surface where light falls and is converted by photoreceptors into neural pulses transmitted to the brain through optical nerves.

[8] For the best experience, the screen in a virtual reality (VR) headset is placed at the focal length of its engineered lens, so that the screen appears to the user as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance.
[9] In a virtual reality (VR) headset, even though the screen appears as a virtual image, a real image is nevertheless formed on the retina, and a person does not perceive the world unless real images are formed on the retina.

Facts:
[1] Sound localization cues are either monaural, involving a single ear, or binaural, involving both ears.
[2] Interaural level difference (ILD) is a binaural sound localization cue that is the difference in sound magnitude heard by each ear, with the ear without obstruction receiving a stronger sound, and the difference can indicate the direction from which the sound is coming.
[3] An acoustic shadow occurs when a sound wave does not reach one ear, caused by an object in front of the sound source or by the position of the head.
[4] Interaural time difference is a binaural sound localization cue from different sound arrival times at the ears; in an average human head, the ears are 21.5 centimeters apart, sound travels that distance in about 0.6 milliseconds, and this small time difference can be used to locate the source.
[5] The auditory component of an extended reality (XR) system should ideally be non-stationary, moving with the user, and interactive, dependent on the listener's actions.
[6] Head-related transfer functions (HRTF) model how a listener receives sound from a location in space, and this model is relevant for dealing with sound in any system, including extended reality (XR) systems.
[7] Head-related transfer functions (HRTF) depend on the size and shape of the head, ears, and ear canal, and every person has a unique HRTF.
[8] Because every person has a unique head-related transfer function (HRTF), it is impractical to determine individual users' HRTFs when building a system, so an HRTF for an average listener is developed and used.
[9] A pair of head-related transfer functions (HRTF) for both ears can be used to synthesize binaural sound, and by generating sound effects or placing sound receivers according to the HRTF, a localization effect can be implemented in an extended reality (XR) system.

[4] The just noticeable difference (JND) is a result from psychophysics that specifies the amount of change in a stimulus that is required for subjects to perceive it as changed in at least 50 percent of trials.
[5] Weber's law captures the just noticeable difference (JND), the change in magnitude that is noticeable, by representing it as delta M divided by M equals C, where M is the magnitude or intensity of the stimulus, delta M is the just noticeable difference, and C is a constant; equivalently, delta M equals M times C.
[6] Weber's law and Stevens' power law are laws from psychophysics that also apply to psychoacoustics, or auditory perception, when physical stimuli are replaced by acoustic stimuli.
[7] For the perceived loudness of a 3000 hertz (Hz) pure tone, the Stevens' power law exponent x is 0.67, so a much higher pressure level is perceived as only a bit louder because the exponent is less than 1.
[8] For a change in a stimulus to be perceived, it must be above the just noticeable difference (JND); for it not to be perceived, it must be within or below the JND.

[5] For smell interfaces, delivering odor near the user's nose for a personal experience is relatively easier than delivering it on a room scale for social or larger experiences, because room-scale delivery generally makes it hard to control odor intensity and uniformity and to vary odor concentration over a large area for localization, which is not easy with current research.
[6] When olfactory displays can generate odor effects, they are shown to induce strong cognitive and emotional responses that make an immersive experience more attractive and more immersive, and pleasant odors can help reduce visually induced motion sickness, also called cybersickness, to some extent.
[7] A taste interface can place electrodes over and under the tongue to provide stimulation that simulates the main taste types.
[8] It is generally difficult to develop taste interfaces without causing people to eat food during the experience, which is not a convenient arrangement and is generally quite difficult to achieve in practice.

[1] Majuli River Island is a river island on the Brahmaputra River in the eastern part of Assam, Northeast India, and it is considered the world's largest inhabited river island and a potential United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) World Heritage Site contender.
[2] Majuli's monsoon season is typically May to September, its non-monsoon season is October to April, and it has an average annual precipitation of 1704 millimeters, an average maximum temperature of 33 degrees Celsius, and a minimum temperature of 7 degrees Celsius.
[3] Majuli's area was about 1250 square kilometers around 1900, had reduced to about 570 square kilometers in 1975, and had further reduced to about 427 square kilometers by 2021, with 2021 data giving about 427.09 square kilometers, an overall reduction of almost two-thirds and about a 25 percent reduction from 1975 to 2021.
[4] Majuli has been constantly hit by severe annual floods and erosion, and river erosion is consuming the island and reducing its habitable area, so formerly habitable areas are no longer habitable and have become sandbars, river banks, underwater areas, or barren areas.
[5] The severe annual floods and erosion of Majuli endanger its cultural resources and its material existence, and although measures are being taken to prevent further erosion, there is a real possibility that the island may disappear.
[6] Satras are Vaishnavite monasteries on Majuli that are authoritative centers of Vaishnavite faith in Assam and are living workshops of different kinds of visual and performing arts.
[7] Majuli is home to several tribal communities, including three distinctive tribal communities—Mising, Deori, and Sonowal Kachari—whose distinctive ways of living, rituals, heritage, and culture make them unique.
[8] Tangible heritage of Majuli consists of heritage aspects that someone can touch and feel, such as cultural artifacts like masks and musical instruments and the architectural aspects of Satras and traditional tribal homes.
[9] Intangible heritage of Majuli consists of heritage aspects that cannot be touched and felt but can be sensed, including traditional skills, knowledge, and aesthetic norms in music, dance forms, drama or performing arts, mask making, vernacular architecture, weaving, food, and agricultural practices, and it is typically embedded in the daily and occasional activities of social life.
[10] Majuli also has ecological heritage, consisting of the flora and fauna that exist because of the island's unique geology, geography, and topography from natural formation.
[11] Before Majuli disappears, it is essential to preserve its tangible heritage, intangible heritage, and ecological heritage.

Facts:
[1] A hand selection technique selects virtual objects in a virtual world with the user's hand by having the user directly reach out to virtually touch the object and trigger a grab; conventionally, selection with hand involves one hand, using a single finger or multiple fingers of one hand.
[2] Hand selection techniques for virtual objects include virtual hand, go-go, prism, and intent-driven selection.
[3] The virtual hand technique is the simplest and most intuitive hand selection technique, in which a visible virtual hand acts as an avatar of the user's physical hand and is tied to it through a one-to-one mapping of the physical hand's motion and orientation, typically implemented with three-dimensional (3D) tracked controllers, allowing natural hand movements.
[4] The virtual hand technique has a problem for selecting distant objects because moving the physical hand to reach them can require a long duration of physical hand movement, which can be tiring and annoying.
[5] The go-go technique is a virtual hand selection technique for distant objects that allows the user to interactively change the virtual arm length, the length of the virtual hand, uses one-to-one mapping when the target is close, and, as distance increases, maps smaller physical hand movements to larger and faster virtual hand movements, possibly exponentially, so that distant objects can be reached quickly.
[6] The go-go technique has a low-precision problem for selecting distant small objects because the virtual hand moves faster when the object is farther away, so a small physical hand movement can miss, bypass, or cross the target and is difficult to control.
[7] The prism technique is an improvement of the go-go technique that applies scaled-down motion to the virtual hand when the user's physical hand moves below a specified speed, and if the hand velocity is slower than a specified minimum velocity, the virtual hand remains still.
[8] For selecting distant objects, prism may provide a better solution than go-go because slowing or stopping the physical hand slows or stops the virtual hand, and the ability to stop the virtual hand when the physical hand stops is not present in go-go.
[9] Prism can result in a mismatch between the real and virtual hand positions because it does not use a one-to-one mapping, which may be counterintuitive.
[10] Intent-driven selection is a hand selection technique in which the user moves the virtual hand toward an object and positions virtual fingers, or uses the posture of virtual fingers, around the object to indicate the user's level of confidence in selecting that object.
[11] Intent-driven selection techniques typically use proximity spheres that encompass multiple objects at a larger distance and progressively reduce in size, depending on hand or finger postures, as the user moves closer to the intended object, refining the selection to a specific object.
[12] In hand selection techniques, go-go and prism are travel techniques, intent-driven selection is a grabbing technique, and intent-driven selection may be combined with a go-go or prism travel technique.

Facts:
[1] Indirect manipulation is a method sometimes used to manipulate virtual objects in which the user does not directly manipulate the virtual object using the physical hand, but instead manipulates other objects mapped to the virtual object, and those other objects in turn manipulate the virtual object.

[2] Three-dimensional (3D) widgets are a simple indirect manipulation technique in which controls are placed directly in the 3D scene with virtual objects, and manipulating a widget manipulates the associated virtual object.

[3] Each three-dimensional (3D) widget is typically responsible for only a small set of manipulation degrees of freedom, so a single widget may not be sufficient to manipulate all properties of a given object; instead, specified sets of degrees of freedom are manipulated using the individual widgets.

[4] Indirect proxies are an indirect manipulation technique that provides a more natural grasping method by letting the user manipulate a local proxy, such as a physical proxy prop linked to a neurological data set, so that moving the proxy moves the linked virtual object in the virtual world.

[5] World in miniature (WIM) is a type of indirect proxy that provides the user with a miniature handheld model of the virtual environment, which represents all objects in the virtual world, so manipulating an object in the miniature model manipulates the corresponding actual object in the virtual world.

[6] World in miniature (WIM) allows manipulation of virtual objects both within and outside the user's reach; for a distant object, the user does not need to select it, but can manipulate its representation in the miniature model, which then manipulates the distant object.

[7] Implementing world in miniature (WIM) for large and complex virtual environments is not very practical because creating the miniature model for such environments is very difficult.

[2] For a given virtual experience, the kind of object selection technique that is suitable is determined by some of the most important parameters or variables that influence user performance while accomplishing the selection task, including the distance of the object to be selected from the current viewpoint or camera position, the direction of the object to be selected, the size of the object to be selected, the density of objects around the target object, and the number of targets to be selected, so that selection performance is maximized.
[3] Target occlusion can also be an important factor in selection performance: if a target is partly occluded by other surrounding objects, locating and selecting it is challenging and specialized techniques may be required, while fully occluded objects may also be selected, but the user must first be made aware of their presence, and specialized selection of fully occluded objects is a special case, with the majority of cases involving partially occluded or partially visible objects.

Facts:
[1] The third category of object selection techniques is image plane or volumetric selection.
[2] Image plane selection, also known as occlusion and framing, is a two-dimensional (2D) selection technique in which the user selects on a view plane that contains the object as viewed from a distance.
[3] In image plane selection, the user holds one or two hands or fingers between the eye and the desired object and provides a signal, such as a gesture or hand movement, to select the object when it lines up with the hand and the eye.
[4] The image plane selection techniques include the head crusher technique, the sticky finger technique, the lifting palm technique, and the framing hands technique, with framing hands being more common and the other techniques less common.
[5] In the head crusher technique, the user positions the thumb and forefinger so that they surround or enclose the desired object in the two-dimensional (2D) image plane.
[6] In the sticky finger technique, the object underneath the user's finger is selected.
[7] In the lifting palm technique, the user selects an object by flattening the outstretched hand and positioning the palm below the desired object as if trying to lift the object with the palm.

Facts:
[1] Walking-based locomotion is a technique for traveling in a virtual environment in which physical walking or movement in the physical world is mapped to corresponding movement in the virtual environment.
[2] Walking-based locomotion is broadly divided into three categories: full gait techniques, partial gait techniques, and gait negation techniques.
[3] In full gait techniques, the user actually walks in the real world and that walk is translated to virtual movement in a virtual environment, which is the most natural way to travel.
[4] In full gait techniques, completely free walking is not practical or possible for virtual navigation, so walking is restricted within a specified limit in the physical space and translated to any amount of movement in a potentially infinite virtual space, creating a mismatch between physical and virtual movement.
[5] In a partial gait technique, the user walks in place, so the user does not change position and is not actually moving forward, backward, left, or right.
[6] Partial gait techniques require specialized devices in addition to other immersive hardware to provide input, may involve active walking interfaces such as pressure mats, pressure sensors, or interfaces with pressure sensors, and map the user's pattern of walking in a single place to different types of walking in the virtual space.
[7] Gait negation techniques require a specialized setup that cancels the user's lateral movements and keeps the user's physical position fixed, because natural walking involves lateral movement that may be difficult to map to a focused virtual movement, and the setup detects and eliminates the lateral movement before the movement is mapped to virtual navigation, making it easier for the system to understand the user's intention.
[8] Some examples of specialized setups used in gait negation techniques are a linear treadmill, motorized floor tiles, a human-sized hamster ball, and a friction-free platform.

Facts:
[1] Selection-based locomotion is a category of locomotion technique in which the user selects where to go rather than continuously specifying how to move there by steering or looking.
[2] Selection-based locomotion has two types: target selection-based locomotion and route planning-based locomotion.
[3] In target selection-based locomotion, the user selects a destination or target, and the virtual viewpoint changes so that the user feels moved to the target.
[4] Target selection-based locomotion techniques include teleportation, which instantly changes the virtual viewpoint from the current location to the target location, map dragging, in which the user fixes a location to move there instantly, and the jumper technique in cave-type systems.
[5] Route planning-based locomotion is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the user selects a route to the target rather than only the endpoint; there may be multiple routes, and while moving through the selected route, different viewpoint changes make the user feel movement along a path, providing more granular control over travel and slightly more natural movement than target-based teleportation.
[6] Manipulation-based locomotion is a category of locomotion technique in which the user's position, orientation, or scale is manipulated using gestures that control either the virtual viewpoint or the virtual world.
[7] Manipulation-based locomotion can be implemented using a combination of the go-go technique, homer technique, and world in miniature metaphor.
[8] In a world in miniature metaphor, moving or manipulating certain objects causes a corresponding change in the virtual viewpoint, as if the user moves from one place to another.

[5] At each place, notifications alert users to available cultural videos; when there is something to see at a spot, the information icon becomes active, and selecting it shows whether a cultural video is available at that spot, which can be played on the tablet interface.
[6] For location awareness, the system uses dual maps: a global map, which is a world-in-miniature map of the entire island, on the tablet interface and a local minimap on the local interface, to reduce clutter and provide clear navigation support.
[7] The global map and the local minimap support wayfinding and orientation awareness by showing the entire world in miniature; the minimap provides dynamic spatial orientation awareness about which direction to move, helping users create a mental map and wayfind.

[1] Navigation has two components: locomotion or travel, which is the motor component, and wayfinding.
[2] Wayfinding refers to location awareness, ascertaining a path through the environment to a desired destination, and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world.
[3] Wayfinding is essentially a mental model, and the goal of wayfinding is to build a mental model or cognitive map of the surroundings and overall environment so that it is easier to locate oneself and identify a suitable path.
[4] The objective of environment design is to make it easier for the user to build a mental map; if the design does not support creation of this mental map, many problems may occur and the overall user experience deteriorates.
[5] The spatial knowledge in a wayfinding mental model consists of landmark knowledge of the surroundings and other places, procedural knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path, and topological or map-like knowledge of the overall environment, together forming the essential knowledge base of the mental model.
[6] A mental model can be created by aiding the user to get, understand, or infer knowledge through the traditional methods of systematic study of a map of a place, exploration of real space, exploration of a copy of the real space or a model of the real space, or any combination of these methods.
[7] For a good immersive user experience in a complex virtual environment with many objects and different ways to reach targets, wayfinding support is essential; locomotion or travel support alone is not sufficient, and regardless of how many or how sophisticated the travel techniques are, without suitable wayfinding support the user cannot use them efficiently or effectively.
[8] Landmark support for wayfinding uses obvious distinct non-mobile objects positioned in a given place, and a good landmark should be clearly visible from several different locations or viewpoints.
[9] Map support for wayfinding can provide maps of the space or place, such as a copy of the virtual world map, where the term world means the virtual world rather than the real world, or a world in miniature display that can show the entire virtual world with objects at different points, the current position of the user, and different routes to different points.
[10] Path following support for wayfinding can denote multiple paths through a single space by colors, so the user knows that there are different paths to reach a destination.
[11] Breadcrumb support for wayfinding leaves a trail of markers along the path followed by predecessors, so users can recognize that a path has already been explored, avoid getting lost, and choose another path or destination to save time.
[12] A compass or another direction indicator can support wayfinding by specifying directions in two-dimensional or three-dimensional space, and a compass can be designed and placed in the environment.

[1] Prototypes can be broadly considered in two categories, horizontal prototypes and vertical prototypes.
[2] A horizontal prototype is a prototype that depicts the entire interface at a surface level, showing how the interface appears to the user in terms of look, feel, and appearance, without any functionality or interaction, so no real work can be done with it.
[3] Horizontal prototypes are suitable for discussing, brainstorming, and eliciting user feedback about the look, feel, and appearance of an interface, including whether its appearance is understandable, intuitive, and usable.
[4] A vertical prototype primarily represents interactions or functionalities by implementing a few selected features likely to be most commonly used in practice, in depth from the first screen to the last screen after the last action is performed, not all functionalities, because that would amount to having the full system.
[5] Vertical prototypes are suitable for analysis of interactions and features because they implement interactions.
[6] In the description of a vertical prototype, the term implemented and the term screen are generic, so implemented does not necessarily mean writing code, and screen can refer to a two-dimensional (2D) computer screen or a scene in a virtual or immersive environment.

Facts:
[1] Quick evaluation of prototypes, also known as expert evaluation, is a technique for quickly and cheaply evaluating a prototype at an early stage of design, unlike a robust evaluation technique, which typically involves suitably skilled evaluators, resources, and an evaluation setup.
[2] The prerequisites for performing quick or expert evaluation are at least a low-fidelity prototype, with higher-quality prototypes being better, and a team of evaluators.
[3] Quick evaluation is a usability test, but although the primary condition of usability testing is to involve users, the evaluation team for quick or expert evaluation is primarily the design team itself or skilled designers with knowledge and skill in the problem domain, and may optionally include a few end users.
[4] Quick or expert evaluation can rely on design-team members or domain experts rather than end users because they are assumed to have user-like experience, their feedback likely reflects users, and engaging them is less complicated, quicker, and cheaper than engaging a full evaluation team with end users.
[5] The evaluation team for expert evaluation should have at least three to five members; more members are welcome, but three to five is sufficient.
[6] In expert evaluation, each evaluator is presented with the prototype, evaluates it independently, and produces a report containing the usability issues perceived by that evaluator; the design team or team lead then combines these reports into a final list of usability issues.

[1] Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert evaluation technique and usability inspection method in which usability problems are identified by inspecting a prototype.
[2] A cognitive walkthrough requires at least a low-fidelity vertical prototype, a prototype that supports several tasks and may be low- or medium-fidelity, and an evaluation team of three to five members; a high-fidelity prototype is more welcome but involves more time and cost.
[3] A low-fidelity prototype for a cognitive walkthrough can be made as simple paper prototypes using the storyboarding approach, in which each prototype is a series of sketches depicting screen changes after each interaction, that is, a storyboard.
[4] In a cognitive walkthrough, a scenario or task description is created for the evaluators, and the task described in the scenario is converted into interface-level tasks, which are the actions that must be performed in the prototype to accomplish that task; the evaluators then perform those actions with the prototype.
[5] Usability questions are framed before a cognitive walkthrough to reflect usability issues, and evaluators use them as guidelines to identify problems users are likely to face while performing the tasks.
[6] For each usability question, evaluators must give a detailed report rather than a simple yes or no answer, explaining where they felt difficulty in the interface or interaction and why.
[7] The evaluators' reports are collected, combined, and analyzed at the end of the evaluation session to identify broader usability issues.

[1] Heuristic evaluation is an evaluation technique in which evaluators assess a presented prototype by ticking items on a checklist of heuristics, without a task scenario or task performance, to perform a comprehensive evaluation of the whole system rather than a task-specific evaluation.
[2] Available checklists for evaluating interfaces include detailed system-specific checklists and checklists focused on broader usability principles, and the broader checklists contain fewer heuristics because they are broader in nature and not specific to any particular interface.
[3] Nielsen's 10 heuristics is a general set of heuristics proposed in 1994 that is primarily related to graphical user interfaces (GUIs) but equally applicable to most interactive systems.
[4] Nielsen's 10 heuristics consist of: 1) visibility of system status, in which the status of the system should be visible to the user; 2) match between system and the real world, in which what the user does on the system should closely match the user's real-world experience; 3) user control and freedom, concerning whether the user is given freedom and what kind of controls are provided; 4) consistency and standards, in which elements and layout should be consistent across different screens and standards should be followed; 5) error prevention, in which the design should help the user prevent errors; 6) recognition rather than recall, in which the user should not have to remember what to do but should be able to recognize from elements what to do because recollection is more difficult than recognition; 7) flexibility and efficiency of use; 8) aesthetic and minimalist design, in which the design should have a minimum number of elements and should be aesthetically pleasing; 9) help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors; and 10) help and documentation, in which the system should provide help and documentation support.
[5] Nielsen's 10 heuristics can be used to identify usability problems at an early stage of design on the basis of simple low-fidelity prototypes, primarily horizontal prototypes, with vertical prototypes optional in heuristic evaluation, unlike the cognitive walkthrough method, where a vertical prototype is mandatory.
[6] Heuristic evaluation requires a team of at least three to five evaluators, who can be members of design teams or other skilled or expert designers not necessarily involved in the design team.
[7] In heuristic evaluation, each evaluator is given the prototype and the checklist of heuristics, evaluates the prototype against each heuristic, reports whether each heuristic is followed or violated and, if violated, gives reasons, and the evaluators' reports are combined and compiled to identify the violated heuristics and major issues.

[1] User evaluation is a quick evaluation technique that obtains feedback by asking users directly, and it requires user involvement, unlike expert evaluation techniques in which user involvement was optional.
[2] User evaluation is often called evaluation with self-reports, and user feedback is collected with rating scales, with the data sometimes called subjective or preference data.

[4] In user evaluation, the items provided to users to rate are questions or statements, and these items are commonly called questionnaires although they need not contain questions.
[5] One major concern in user evaluation is that identifying suitable questionnaires is challenging.
[6] In user evaluation, data can be collected after every task and at the end of the session, collecting data at both points is desirable if feasible, otherwise one of the two points must be chosen, and suitable questionnaires must be created for the point at which data are collected, so the questionnaires used after every task need not be the same as those used after the whole session.
[7] Well-known questionnaires available for post-task data collection include the After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ), designed by Lewis in 1991, and the Expectation Measure (EM), designed by Albert and Dixon in 2003.
[8] Well-known questionnaires available for post-session data collection include the System Usability Scale (SUS), designed by Brooke in 1996; the Computer System Usability Questionnaire (CSUQ), designed by Lewis in 1995; the Questionnaire for User Interface Satisfaction (QUIS), designed by Chin et al. in 1988; and the Usefulness Satisfaction and Ease of Use questionnaire (USE), proposed by Lund in 2001.

[6] To balance the trade-off between testability and generalization, stage 1 of an empirical study frames multiple testable research questions covering different aspects of a system and combines their conclusions to reach a definitive conclusion about a broader untestable generalized question, such as the overall goodness of an interface.

Facts:
[1] In an experimental study, tasks can be assigned using a within-subject (repeated measures) design, in which every participant performs the tasks corresponding to all test conditions, or a between-subjects design, in which the tasks for all test conditions are divided and distributed among subsets of participants.
[2] Within-subject designs are easier to manage than between-subject designs, but choosing between them depends on circumstances, such as the availability of participants and resources, which may force a between-subject design.
[3] In a within-subject design, the practice effect is an improvement in task performance from repeated practice; it is also called a confounding variable and confounds the analysis by adding noise to the data, because performance gains may be due to practice rather than to the interface.
[4] To reduce the practice effect in a within-subject design, the task sequence can be randomized or systematically varied; statistically, these random or systematic variations are supposed to nullify the practice effect.
[5] A Latin square design systematically varies the task sequence allocated to each participant, for example by shifting a numbered task sequence one position for each successive participant.

[6] Because the Majuli VR Tour application was 5.1 gigabytes (GB) and not suitable for mobile deployment, a mobile version for Google Cardboard was made by compressing high-resolution 360-degree and two-dimensional (2D) images and removing most video playback support, reducing the application size to 0.7 gigabytes (GB).
[7] The Oculus Quest version of the Majuli VR Tour used 597 images, 11 cultural videos, 8 drone videos, and 5 360-degree videos, while the Google Cardboard mobile version used all 597 images in compressed form, no cultural videos, no drone videos, and 1 360-degree video for the initial experience.

[1] The empirical study was conducted to collect real-life data of a user moving from one point to another and to propose a speed estimation model.
[2] The empirical study involved 40 participants, comprising 26 male and 14 female participants, aged 19 to 42 years.
[3] In the empirical study, participant heights were recorded because earlier studies indicate that height affects walking behavior, and the participants' heights ranged from 150 to 184 centimeters.
[4] The corridor experiment used a corridor in a physical building in which seven paintings representing images of the seven wonders of the world were placed at distances of 20, 20, 13, 16, 6.4, 19, and 4 meters from the start.
[5] The seven paintings simulated points of interest in a system-controlled virtual tour, where a user may need to stop, pause, and then move.
[6] Participants were instructed to start walking from the starting place and stop at each painting to click a photograph, a task assigned to ensure that the user stopped after walking a predefined distance.
[7] Video recordings of the user's footsteps were made with a Samsung M30 smartphone camera fixed on the user's back and focused on the user's legs; the recording started just before the user started walking and was captured at 30 frames per second.

[1] The first stage of the travel-time algorithm is to compute the time to travel between two directly connected nodes using the natural walking-speed model.
[2] In the natural walking-speed model, perceived instantaneous walking speed is the visual gain of 2.1 multiplied by the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act).
[3] Because speed is dx/dt, the instantaneous time dt for a distance element dx is dx divided by 2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act), and the total travel time over a distance D between directly connected nodes is the integral from 0 to D of dx/(2.1 V act).
[4] In the natural walking-speed model, f is the instantaneous step frequency and h is the height of the user.
[5] After solving the integral with simplifications, rearrangements, and Fourier-series expansion up to n0, the travel-time estimate tau D for a directly connected vertex pair under the natural walking model is D/V naught times (3 - (16/pi^2) * sum_{k=1}^{n0} 1/(2k-1)^2).
[6] V naught is a constant for a given height h, equal to 2.1 h^2 divided by (0.157 * 1.72^2 * 1.8^2), where h is the user's height.

Facts:
[1] The algorithm takes the original graph G, with vertex set V and edge set epsilon, as input and produces the optimal time T and the path P of the minimum-time path that covers all vertices in G.
[2] The algorithm first converts the original graph G into a complete graph G' by keeping every directly connected edge unchanged and, for each pair of vertices that is not directly connected, adding a hypothetical edge whose length is the shortest path between those vertices in G.
[3] After the graph is complete, the algorithm replaces the Euclidean-distance edge weights with the travel time between each pair of vertices, producing a complete time-weighted graph G'' whose edge weights are travel times rather than Euclidean distances.
[4] The complete time-weighted graph G'' can be solved with a standard travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver, without needing a new algorithm, and the solver returns the optimal time tau_opt and the optimal path p_opt for that modified graph.

Facts:
[1] There are two approaches to minimizing the possibility of cybersickness in a virtual world: finding a path that covers all points of interest in minimum time, and finding a path that covers the maximum possible points of interest within a given time limit.
[2] In the minimum-time approach, the virtual world is represented as a graph whose nodes are points of interest, whose directly connected edges are weighted by the Euclidean distance between the corresponding points of interest, and whose graph need not be complete.
[3] The problem of finding the minimum-duration travel that covers all points of interest in the virtual-world graph is mapped to the travelling salesman problem (TSP), a standard classical problem.
[4] In the minimum-time approach, travel times between pairs of vertices are computed using the natural walking speed model, so if the vertices are directly connected the model gives the travel time between them, and if they are not directly connected a hypothetical edge representing the shortest path between them is introduced and the travel time along that shortest path is computed using the model.
[5] In the minimum-time approach, the computed travel times become the weights of a complete graph formed by adding hypothetical edges, and this complete graph is given as input to a travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver, which outputs the optimum time and optimal path.
[6] The optimal path produced by the travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver may contain hypothetical edges, which must be removed before the final solution path is produced.
[7] The minimum-time approach that covers all points of interest may still produce a travel time beyond the threshold beyond which cybersickness may occur, motivating the use of a time limit in the alternative path optimization approach.

[1] The input to the optimal-path algorithm for a virtual environment is the original graph G, which is a fully connected graph but not necessarily a complete graph, with vertex set V, edge set E, and importance f and waiting time w specified for each node.
[2] The desired output of the algorithm is the optimal path P that maximizes the importance value F, covers the maximum number of most important points of interest (POIs), and keeps the total exposure time, i.e. the traveling time plus the waiting time, less than the time threshold.
[3] The first stage of the algorithm is to compute the complete graph G dash by replacing every pair of vertices that is not directly connected with the shortest path between those vertices.
[4] The algorithm then replaces the edge weights in the complete graph, which are originally the Euclidean distances between node pairs, with travel times t computed using the natural walking model, producing the final graph G double dash, whose edges are weighted by travel duration to give a realistic experience.
[5] The final graph G double dash, together with the importance f and waiting time w of each node, is given as input to a virtual reality path planning (VRPP) solver, and the solver returns the optimal path P_opt.
[6] The optimal path returned by the solver is modified by replacing each hypothetical edge between vertices V_i and V_j with the shortest path between those vertices in the original graph, and the algorithm returns this modified optimal path.

Facts:
[1] Extended reality (XR), in particular virtual reality (VR), is resource hungry, meaning that XR and VR require a lot of resources.
[2] The objectives of virtual reality (VR) resource optimization are to minimize resource requirements without compromising the VR experience, that is, to maximize the VR experience.
[3] In extended reality (XR) and particularly in virtual reality (VR), resources can include any or all of hardware, software, manpower, and supporting infrastructure; in VR these include hardware such as input devices, processing devices, and output devices; software such as development tools, software development kits, software packages, or application packages; manpower such as staff for development, deployment, maintenance, and marketing; and supporting infrastructure such as rooms to store the hardware setup, electricity supply, furniture, and network infrastructure such as network gear, switches, routers, wires, and servers.
[4] Each resource type in extended reality (XR) can be optimized separately, but such optimization is not easy because the considerations vary widely and include money such as availability of funds and how resources are managed, availability of the resources before use, policy issues, and geopolitical issues.
[5] Virtual reality (VR) resource optimization generally does not try to optimize every resource, assumes some resources are given, and instead focuses on hardware requirements at the client end (the user end), because focusing on client-end hardware is the most straightforward way to optimize resources without being entangled in many issues; the objective is for the end user to have a good experience with affordable hardware resources.

[1] A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller.
[2] In a generic graphics system, the host computer, or its central processing unit (CPU), has two-way communication with the display controller, in which the CPU sends display commands and may receive interaction data.
[3] The display controller is responsible for image generation, meaning it creates a representation of a scene as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed on a two-dimensional screen.
[4] Image generation is a multi-stage computational process, and if all rendering-related computations were carried out by the central processing unit (CPU), the CPU's time would be consumed by rendering, leaving it with very little time for other tasks and the system could do little except rendering; to avoid this and increase efficiency, rendering is usually carried out by a dedicated component.
[5] The dedicated rendering component is typically the graphics card, which usually contains its own graphics processing unit (GPU); in a generic graphics system this component is called the display controller, and the central processing unit (CPU) passes graphics rendering tasks to it so the computation takes place in the GPU rather than in the CPU.
[6] The display controller generates the image in a digital format, as strings of zeros and ones, and sends that image representation to video memory for storage.
[7] Video memory is the dedicated part of the overall memory hierarchy of the computer where the digital image is stored, typically as part of a separate graphics unit, and in modern graphics cards it is sometimes called video random-access memory (VRAM).
[8] A graphic display screen generally has a grid of picture elements, or pixels; when these pixels are activated, or excited, by an electrical or electromechanical means, they emit light with specific intensities that the viewer perceives as a colored image on the screen.
[9] The video controller uses the data stored in video memory to render an image on the screen, converting the digital image into some analog voltages required to activate the pixels, and it controls the pixel excitation mechanism using the video memory content.

[1] Space partitioning representation is a broad category of object representation in which the three-dimensional (3D) space occupied by an object is divided into several disjoint, non-overlapping regions, so that any point inside the object lies in exactly one region and the object can be represented by representing the occupied regions.
[2] A space partitioning tree is a hierarchical, tree-like structure that represents the space occupied by an object and is used to create a space partitioning representation.
[3] Space partitioning representations include the octree method, binary space partitioning, and constructive solid geometric methods.
[4] Specialized sophisticated representation techniques are often required for application-specific or very complex photorealistic objects rather than the broader boundary or space partitioning categories.
[5] Fractal representation is a specialized representation method for self-repeating structures, such as a leaf whose individual parts repeat in the larger part.
[6] Particle system representation is a specialized representation method for objects such as a waterfall that relies on the simulation of physical properties.
[7] A skeletal model is a specialized representation method for complex characters such as a cat that captures the character's overall appearance and motion behavior, and such models are typically used in animation or computer animation to represent objects or complex characters.

[2] In the worked example, transforming rectangle ABCD from its local coordinate system to the chimney-like shape A′, B′, C′, D′ in the world coordinate scene cannot be done with one basic transformation and requires two basic transformations, scaling and translation.

[4] A composite transformation matrix is formed by arranging the individual transformation matrices from right to left according to the order of application: the first transformation applied is placed rightmost, each subsequent transformation is placed to its left, and the matrices are multiplied.
[5] In the worked example involving rectangle ABCD and A′, B′, C′, D′, scaling is applied first and translation is applied second, so the translation matrix is placed to the left of the scaling matrix and the two matrices are multiplied to obtain the composite transformation matrix.

[7] Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so the right-to-left sequence of transformations must be set correctly; an incorrect sequence may produce an incorrect transformed result.

Facts:
[1] A window is the same as a normalized clipping window, is another term for the view plane, and is an abstract intermediate representation that has nothing to do with the display.
[2] A viewport is not defined on the view plane but in device space as a portion of the final screen where the scene will be rendered, and it is defined with respect to the screen or display origin and the screen or display dimensions.
[3] The window-to-viewport transformation maps a point from the abstract window representation to a device-specific viewport representation, specifically from a window point (Wx, Wy) to a viewport point (Vx, Vy).
[4] In the window-to-viewport transformation, the transformation matrix is a three by three matrix whose Sx is defined in terms of the viewport and window dimensions along the x-axis, whose Sy is similarly defined with respect to the viewport and window dimensions along the y-axis, and whose Tx and Ty are computed in terms of Sx and Sy and the corresponding x-axis or y-axis window and viewport dimensions.
[5] To obtain the transformed viewport point, the window point vector is multiplied by the window-to-viewport transformation matrix, and because the resulting point is in homogeneous coordinate representation, the Cartesian point is obtained by dividing the result by the homogeneous factor W.

[2] A naive line-rendering method requires many floating-point operations, and because floating-point operations slow down a computer, the objective of efficient line-rendering algorithms is to avoid floating-point operations.
[3] Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm is a popular line-rendering algorithm that identifies the pixels that approximately represent a line without using floating-point operations.
[4] The Bresenham line-drawing algorithm is described for line slopes between -1 and +1, with minor modification needed for other slopes; its input is the two line endpoints and its output is the set of pixels that approximate the line segment.
[5] In Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm for line slopes between -1 and +1, the algorithm first computes delta x, the difference between the two endpoints' x coordinates, delta y, the difference between their y coordinates, and the decision parameter p, defined as twice delta y minus delta x; it initializes x and y to the first endpoint's x and y coordinates and adds that pixel to the output pixel set; then, in a loop until the other endpoint is reached, if p is less than 0 it increments x by 1 and resets p to the older p plus twice delta y, otherwise increments x and y by 1 and resets p to the older p plus twice delta y minus twice delta x, adding each computed coordinate to the output pixel set.
[6] Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm is efficient and speeds up line rendering because it uses integer arithmetic, such as addition and multiplication, and avoids floating-point operations such as rounding, division, and sometimes floating-point multiplication.
[7] Speeding up line rendering makes the system more efficient because at any instant a system may need to render a large number of line segments, and in interactive graphics such as virtual reality each user input can change the scene and require redrawing hundreds of thousands of lines.
[8] Similar efficient rendering algorithms exist for other geometric shapes, such as circles, ellipses, filled areas, and polygons, and they are more complex than line rendering.
[9] The basic idea for rendering a shape on a screen is to map the original shape to the set of pixels that represent it as fast as possible by reducing floating-point operations.
[10] For lines, floating-point operations can be completely eliminated, whereas for other shapes they may not be completely eliminated but can be minimized.
